MOTIONS
New Zealand Defence Force—Deaths of Lance Corporals Pralli Durrer and Rory
Malone in Afghanistan

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion
without notice on the in cident on Saturday, 4 August 201 2 in the Bamian Province of
Afghanistan that tragically claimed the lives  of two New Zealand soldiers and injured
six more.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That this House express  its deep sympathy and
condolences to the family, friends, and milita ry colleagues of the New Zealand Army
soldiers killed in Afghanistan on 4 August, and  also express its sy mpathy to their six
injured colleagues and its best wishes for their recovery.  On Saturday, 4 August at
around 8 a.m. local time memb ers of the New Zealand De fence Force’s provincial
reconstruction team responded to a request for assistance from an Afghan quick reaction
force platoon, which had come under insurg ent attack in north- east Bamian. A New
Zealand Defence Force patrol was immediately mobilised and assisted in engaging the
insurgents until a second New Zealand Defence Force patrol arrived. It too came under
attack, during which some of our personne l were wounded. Two further New Zealand
patrols arrived, and during the ensuing fi re fight the New Zealand Defence Force
sustained more casualties, including Lance Corporal Rory Malone, who was killed at
the scene. Seven wounded were evacuated, and the most seriously injured soldier,
Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer, died en route to hospital.
This incident has served as a tragic reminder of the risks that our men and women in
the services face every day in unstable conflict zones. Rory Malone and Pralli Durrer
are the sixth and seventh Kiwis to die wh ile working selflessly on behalf of New
Zealand and the international community in trying to stabilise Afghanistan. These Kiwis
are willing to risk their lives defending not their homeland but strangers in another
country. We could not ask more of them. We could not expect more of them.
The Government has received messages from  many other Governments and leaders
who understand the terrible sacrifices that  are being made in Afghanistan as we
collectively do our best to cr eate a functioning, stable society there. We have always
known that the task is both vital and dange rous. I know that for the Defence Force and
their families, accepting that there are risks in  the job is part of daily life. However, I
also know that that knowledge does not make it any easier when the knock at the door
that they hope will never come does come . The weekend before last it came for the
Durrers and the Malones, and also for their friends and colleagues inside and outside the
Defence Force, and for the Government and the people of New Zealand. On Saturday I
attended the memorial service for Pralli Du rrer and Rory Malone, and the more I learn
about them, the more heavily their loss weighs.
We are mindful today also of the injured. I am advised that three of the six returned
to their families in New Zealand late yesterday. Three more remain in hospital in
Germany, all in a stable condition. One of them is Major Craig Wilson, who was the
commanding officer of the team involved in the attack. He has strongly praised the
courage and the performance of Lance Cor porals Durrer and Malone in the combat
4290 Motions 14 Aug 2012
engagement that claimed their lives. It is hard to find any redeeming feature in this
tragedy, but at least in  today’s conflicts we ar e usually able to repa triate our fallen, and
the Government thanks the United States G overnment for its assistance in evacuating
the wounded and returning Rory Malone and Pralli Durrer to their families.
Bamian is a better place because of the de dication, effort, and commitment of these
men and their colleagues. Their sacrifice has been a dreadful price to pay, but a
reminder too of why we are there. Violence,  lawlessness, and a brutal and wilful
disregard of the rights of others should neve r be allowed to become a way of life. These
two young, brave men were fighting for a more secure Afghanistan and a more secure
world. We are proud of them and their colleag ues, who right now as I speak are facing
the same risks to uphold the same noble objectives. The Malone and Durrer families’
loss is New Zealand’s loss. We grieve for them and with them.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: On Saturday I attended the
memorial service for the two brave, young Ne w Zealand soldiers who tragically lost
their lives on 4 August while serving in Afghanistan. It was a moving experience to
hear the families of Lance Co rporal Pralli Durrer and Lance Corporal Rory Malone talk
about the contribution these men made to th eir communities, to the Defence Force, and
to our country. Both of their commanders s poke also of their enthusiasm in the army
and the respect they earned from their mates who served alongside them. Their families
are proud of them and so are we as a nation.
Rory Malone is remembered as a quiet st udent with a wicked sense of humour who
just got on with things. His steady determination continued when he entered the army in
2002. His great-great-grandfather Lieutenant Colonel William Malone was the
commanding officer of the Wellington Infantry  Battalion at Gallipoli who died at
Chunuk Bair. He led his troops with much bravery. Rory showed the same family
courage under fire. He repor tedly dragged his company co mmander to safety before,
sadly, losing his life helping another fallen comrade caught up in the battle.
Pralli Durrer was a Southern Man, born in Invercargill, growing up in Christchurch.
He is still remembered at his primary school  as being a shining star. He survived the
initial attacks, supporting his comrades under fire. Sadly, he was wounded, and passed
away en route to the base at Bagram.
These soldiers made the ultimate sacrifice. They lost their lives doing what they
believed in, and we will  always remember them for that . They are our heroes. Six other
New Zealand soldiers were also injured in the attack. We wish them a speedy recovery.
We also thank the Dutch, German, and American  air forces, which came to their aid in
the aftermath of the attack.
The deaths of these two young men come al most exactly 2 years to the day since
New Zealand’s first fatality in Afghanistan, when Lieutenant Tim O’Donnell was killed
in the same area during an attack on his patrol . It is fitting that we remember him today,
along with all those New Zealanders who have died in Afghanistan and in other conflict
zones around the world, serving our country. Th ey gave their lives trying to make the
world a better place.
Often these soldiers make an impact that  is largely unseen. We look at the Bamian
Province. How many kids are alive today simply because their work allowed
vaccinations to happen? How many women surv ived childbirth because stability in the
province brought about by their efforts ensure d those women could get to hospital? Or
the numbers of children—especially girls—who have attended school and now have
possibilities for a much better life, more than they had before.
We thank our soldiers for doing us pr oud, for contributing to peace, and for
contributing to making a better world. We re spect and honour the sacrifice they have
14 Aug 2012 Motions 4291
made, we mourn their loss, and we will neve r forget them. Our prayers and sympathies
today are with their families. Rest in peace.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Green Party stands to acknowledge the
sacrifice that Lance Corporal  Pralli Durrer and Lance Corp oral Rory Patrick Malone
made as members of the provi ncial reconstruction team in  Afghanistan. Both men have
been taken from us far too young, at 26 years of  age. This loss, the greatest loss of life
and injury in active New Zealand service since Viet Nam, is felt throughout the country.
We also acknowledge those who were injured in the same action. We wish them a rapid
recovery, and know that everything possible will be done to assist them in their physical
and psychological recovery.
It takes courage to put one’s  life on the line in the service of New Zealand and of
humanity. We acknowledge the dedication, the skill, and the bravery of both men. Both
had served overseas before, assisting with the stabilisation force during times of trouble
in Timor-Leste. Our thoughts are with the men’s families and their larger wh ānau at this
sad time. I was privy to their powerful a nd moving statements of love and loss at
Burnham on Saturday, and to the invincible haka and the haunting bagpipes that sent
Pralli and Rory on their final journey. May those grieving today be comforted in the
knowledge that the pride in which they held their loved ones is shared by the rest of this
nation.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand
First, I wish to express our condolences and utmost sympathy to the families and friends
of Lance Corporal Rory Malone and Lan ce Corporal Pralli Durrer. The questionable
issue of the continued positioning of our soldiers in Afghanistan should wait for another
day. Today it is appropriate that we all join, in this country and in this House, to pay our
respects to these men, and their families and friends. They have made the ultimate
sacrifice on behalf of this country. We also wish a qu ick recovery to those comrades-in-
arms who were injured alongside both Lance Corporals Malone and Durrer.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Mr Speaker, tēnā koe. Tū
ana au ki te tautoko i ng ā mihi kua mihia, ng ā poroporoaki ō tātau o te Whare nei ki a
rāua a Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer, a La nce Corporal Rory Malone, i hinga mai r āua i
te pakanga i Afghanistan. I a r āua e hōia ana, e mahi ana kua puta mai te karanga i t ērā
rōpū hōia o Aotearoa kia haere ake ki te āwhina, ki te tautoko i t ētahi rōpū pirihimana o
Afghanistan e raruraru ana i te pakanga. Haere ake te r ōpū o Aotearoa ki te pakanga. I
taua pakanga i Do Abe, ka hinga mai a Pral li, ka hinga mai a Rory. Ka whara kino hoki
ētahi o ō rāua hoa kei te h ōhipera rātau i t ēnei wā. Nā reira, kua whakahokia mai ng ā
tūpāpaku ki Aotearoa nei, ki Burnham. I t ū mai te tangihanga i te R āhoroi kua pahure
ake.
I tae atu ētahi ō mātau ngā mema o te P āremata nei ki taua tangihanga, i kite m ātau i
te whanaungatanga i waenga i ng ā hōia o T ūmatauenga i t ērā rā. I rongo m ātau i ng ā
kōrero a ngā āpiha o Tūmatauenga, e kōrero ana mō ngā mahi toa kua oti e ēnei tokorua.
I kite hoki m ātau i ng ā āpiha me ng ā whānau e t ū ana ki te k ōrero ki a r ātau. Ko Pralli
nō Ng āti Kahungunu n ā reira, i hui tahi m ātau me ng ā wh ānau i reira. K ī mai r ātau e
harikoa ana r ātau ki te kite i ētahi mema P āremata i tae atu ki t ērā tangihanga ki te
tautoko i a r ātau. N ā reir ā, ko taku k ōrero ki a r āua kia haere ake me ng ā kōrero i te
mōhio kua oti pai tā rātau mahi mō tō tātau whenua o Aotearoa nei. Ka mau tonu ā rātau
kōrero, ā rātau mahi kei roto i te hītori o tēnei whenua o Aotearoa.
Nā reira, kōrua tahi, haere. Haere kohikohingia ng ā tini mate o ng ā marae maha o te
motu, kia tae pai koutou ki mua i te aroaro o te Kaihanga. N ā reira, ko koutou ērā, ko
mātau ēnei e tangi atu nei. Kai te tokorua, haere, haere, haere atu rā.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker. I rise to endorse our acknowledgments and the
farewell tributes of this House to those two, Lance Corporal Pr alli Durrer and Lance
4292 Motions 14 Aug 2012
Corporal Rory Malone, who lost their lives  in a battle in Afghani stan. While they were
serving and performing their duties a call went out to th e New Zealand Defence Force
to provide assistance and suppor t for the Afghanistan police force in d ifficulties in a
battle. In that attack in Do Abe Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer and Lance Corporal Rory
Malone were killed, and some of th eir colleagues were badly wounded and are
currently in hospital. The bodies were brought back to Burnham Military Camp and the
funeral took place last Saturday.
Some of us members of Parliament attended that funeral, where we witnessed that
sense of family connection among the army so ldiers that day. We heard the speeches by
army officers about the acts of bravery displayed and achieved by these two. We also
observed officers and families standing and talking with each other. Because Pralli
Durrer was from Ng āti Kahungunu we and the family met there. They said to us how
pleased they were to see some members of Pa rliament at that funeral to support them. I
said to them to come up with their storie s, knowing full well that the two soldiers had
served this country of ours, Aotearoa, well.
And so to you two, depart. Go forth and gat her up the many deaths from the vast
number of courtyards of the nation to ensure  that you as a collective arrive before the
Creator. So you are they, and we are these one s here who mourn you. Therefore, to you
two in particular, I bid you farewell, farewell, and go forth.]

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I rise today on behalf of the ACT Party to
pay our respects to Lance Corporals Pralli  Durrer and Rory Malone, both 26, who died
serving our country in an inhospitable a nd dangerous place on Saturday 2 weeks past.
We offer our heartfelt condolen ces to their families and friends at this very difficult
time. A mum’s boy, a father’s son—no words can ever take away the pain of their loss.
But we hope they can find some solace in the country’s recognition of their sons’ heroic
contribution.
The young men and women who choose to jo in the army do so knowing the high
risks and inherent dangers of the job, but they choose to do so willingly. On the gates of
Burnham Military Camp in Christchurch th e following words are written: “Remember
that prosperity can only be fo r the free, and that freedom is  the sure possession of those
alone who have the courage to defend it.” Lance Corporal Durrer and Lance Corporal
Malone, ordinary men who demonstrated ex traordinary courage, died doing exactly
that.
Hearing their colleagues speak about them was to know they were both men of much
humour, much fun, and much wit. Their brav ery came from their families. The shared
values of loyalty, commitment,  and patriotism were inhe rent in thei r background, and,
indeed, their sense of duty a nd sacrifice came from their great-great-grandfathers. Some
of the greatest battles in history have defi ned this nation’s char acter, from Cassino, to
Guadalcanal, to Afghanistan—across the world, a century of sacrifice and tragedy. This
country stands apart for our role in the global destiny of freedom and peace, and the
common thread is young soldiers prepared  and ready to go to defend our fragile
democracy.
At this time, we are also thinking of Major Craig Wilson, the commander of the New
Zealand troops caught in the ambush at Bamian Province, and their five comrades who
were seriously wounded. We acknowledge and salute their bravery on this fateful day, 4
August 2012. We wish them well.
For the fallen, Lance Corporal Durrer and Lance Corporal Malone:
They went with songs to the battle, they were young,
Straight of limb, true of eye, steady and aglow.
They were staunch to the end against odds uncounted,
14 Aug 2012 Motions 4293
They fell with their faces to the foe.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Yet again we take time out from
this House to pay tribute to the memory of brave, talented, and able young New
Zealanders who have lost  their lives in a field of conflic t as horrific, as barren, and as
desperate as Afghanistan. T oday we pay rightful tribut e to Lance Corporals Rory
Malone and Pralli Durrer, and we acknowledg e the sense of loss that their comrades,
their friends, and their families will be feeling at the circumstances of their deaths.
I think it is time to reca ll also the memories we have every Anzac Day, when we
think about those brave soldiers a century ago who, against incredible odds, made the
remarkable sacrifices that th ey did. We marvel about th eir bravery, we marvel about
their maturity, and we marvel about their sense of duty and accomplishment. These two
young men epitomise that spir it. We need marvel no longer. We have seen it
demonstrated in our soldiers, in the work th ey have done in Afghanistan, and, sadly, in
the sacrifices they have made. It is a historical coincidence that in the case of Lance
Corporal Malone there is a linka ge back to that gr eat conflict at Gallipoli. But, in every
sense, Lance Corporals Durrer and Malone are the modern embodiment of that Anzac
spirit.
Although our words give due solemnity to the occasion, and although our words
speak for the nation in the sense of paying it s tribute to those men, they will be only a
form of comfort to the families who have to live now constantly with the loss. But
maybe there is some consolation in memor y. Maybe there is some consolation in the
high regard that these young me n were obviously held in, a nd the gratitude that this
country feels for their service and for their contribution. May they rest in peace.
Motion agreed to.
2012 Olympic Games—Success of New Zealand Team

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: I seek leave to
move a motion without notice congratula ting the members of the 2012 New Zealand
Olympic Team.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: I move, That this House congrat ulate the members of
the 2012 New Zealand Olympic team on their outstanding performance, achieving six
gold medals, two silver, and five bronze,  and finishing ranked 15th in the world . I
believe that by any standards the 2012 Ne w Zealand Olympic campaign can be judged
to have been a substantial success. I want to, on behalf of the Government, acknowledge
all of the athletes who were members of that team and congratulate them collectively on
their achievement. In particular, I want to congratulate the 13 athletes or teams that won
medals.
I was present in London for 3 or 4 days, and the overwhelming impression that you
got was one of the level of difficulty, th e sheer pressure to perform in such a
challenging environment. For our people to have succeeded on such a scale against very
difficult odds is a very signi ficant achievement indeed. Six gold medals—one of which
came along a little later than the others—two silver, and five bronze are an outstanding
achievement by any standards. It places New Zealand 15 th overall on the tally of
Olympic medals achieved in 2012, and on a per capita basis—and I think it is worth
doing this piece of arithmetic from time to ti me—I understand that we finished fourth
by comparison with all other countries.
4294 Motions 14 Aug 2012
I want to recognise that this effort was so mething that was shared by more than just
those who performed on the field. I want to recognise the coaches, the support staff, and
the families, who played such an important part in our Olympic performance. Although
it is always difficult to single out any indi vidual achievement, I do want to note the
achievement of the rowing head coach, Dick Tonks, whose previous successes on the
international stage are well known, but whose success at the 2012 Olympics was simply
remarkable.
I think it is fitting that we should recognise that many members of the team achieved
personal milestones—some, personal bests—and it is worth noting that by the end of
the games New Zealand participants had achieved 35 top eight finishes and 72 in the top
16. All of this leaves New Zealand well plac ed for Rio in 2016. I think it is reasonably
well known that we are part-way through a major expansion of high performance
facilities and services towards enhancing ta rgeted sports selected by High Performance
Sport New Zealand. The notable feature of these games was the outstanding success of
the rowers, who have had the benefit of world-class high performance facilities for most
of the build-up period, and outstanding coaching and support services. If we are able to
achieve, on the strength of the enhanced f acilities and services  now embarked upon,
anything like the return that we have seen from rowing at these games, that augurs
extremely well for the future. Again, I o ffer, on behalf of the Government, our
congratulations to all of the members of the 2012 Olympic team.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: It has been an outstanding
Olympics, and I want to join with Mr McCully in congratulating our team on its
fantastic effort. We have been richly reward ed for those efforts w ith 13 medals. Six of
those are gold, and I was—along  with everybody else in th is House—thrilled to see
Valerie Adams trade her silver in for a gold fi rst thing this morning. It was justice after
all of the effort that she has gone through over the past weeks.
Our rowers have done us particularly pr oud, and I too want to acknowledge Dick
Tonks and his efforts for the rowing team . I single out Mahe Drysdale because I
remember 4 years ago his being sick but ge tting across the line for a bronze medal, and
in this Olympics he was rewarded with a gold. Their success on the water is richly
deserved. Rowing is a well-orga nised sport that has worked hard to attract  and nurture
young and talented students.
Our sailors have performed outstanding ly, along with Lisa Carrington in the
canoeing, and watching Sarah Walker was an inspiration as she overcame her fears to
take the silver medal in that mad dash on her BMX. Our equestrian team always does us
proud, and once again represented New Zeala nd with distinction. Our cyclists blew
away their opponents with an exciting performance that saw them take home bronze
medals as well.
We are proud of all the New Zealanders who represented us at the London games. It
has been a real triumph and ha s lifted the spir its of an entire count ry. Many of us have
been so caught up with this that we have come rather bleary-eyed to work. I have to say
that I have turned up late to a few meetings , but explained that I had been watching the

items.speaker: Olympics and they said
items.text: “Oh, that’s OK then.” We have lost that excuse, unfortunately.
We managed to win only one gold 12 year s ago at the 2000 Olympics, and it has
been a complete turn-round sin ce that time. It is a result of a commitment to develop,
invest in, and grow our high performance sports. This has taken some time and a long-
term commitment to sport. It involves growing interest at a grassroots level, identifying
and investing in young talent, e xposing our sportspeople to international competition,
and using the best training methods to allow them to achieve at this highest level.
I also want to pay tribute to the work of New Zealander David Holman. Many of you
may not know who he is, but he is the dire ctor of the World Anti-Doping Agency, or
14 Aug 2012 Motions 4295
WADA. The World Anti-Doping Agency plays a key role in making sure our sports are
clean and our athletes can compete fairly  in a doping-free sporting environment. We
thank David Hoffman for this work, and—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Howman.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: —Howard, sorry—for establishi ng New Zealand as a world
leader in anti-doping.
We are proud of our athletes and the spirit in which they compete. We thank them for
their tremendous effort in London, but we also  thank all those who stand beside them:
their families, their coaches, and the organi sations that support them. In fact, it is
important to take a moment to thank all those New Zealanders who are involved in
sports at every level. They give up their time, their week ends with family, and their
energy because they love their sport. Their commitment allows us to develop athletes
who are amongst the best in the world, an d we have seen the outcome of that
commitment on the podiums in London over the past few weeks. Thank you to the
entire Olympic team and all those who s upported it for making these Olympics such a
great one.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: On behalf of the Green Party I want to join other
parties—and, I am sure, New Zealand Firs t as well, shortly—in welcoming home our
Olympians and congratulating them on a fantastic effort. It has been a great Olympics. I
think Britain did a superb job of hosting the games, starting with Danny Boyle’s “camp-
tastic” opening ceremony and right through until the close of the games this week, and
all of our athletes have done us proud. This is arguably ou r best ever Olympic Games,
because I think most of us would put an asterisk next to the Los Angeles Olympic
Games, with all of the countries that stay ed away. I think the e ffort this year has
eclipsed that one.
My personal favourite moments from the games were Nathan Cohen and Joseph
Sullivan pulling it out in that last 500 metres to take out the double sculls, and Jack
Bauer’s effort in the men’s road race—fantastic. But, as the Minister for Sport and
Recreation said, it is invidious  to select individuals, and those are just my personal
choices.
Although winning medals of course feel s good, I was most impressed with the
gracious, modest, and heartfel t comments made by all of our  Olympians, either in
winning or in defeat. I believe that that is the mark of true champions, and all of our
team did us proud in that regard.
I am looking forward to the Paralympian t eam’s efforts, which are coming up, and,
hopefully, we will also as a nation share in the joy and the triumph of that team.
I want to close with the words of our  silver medal - winning BMX racer, Sarah
Walker. She said that being from a small town does not matter; it is possible to dream
big and achieve those dreams. It is our job here in this House to enable all of our kids to
be able to dream big, and to empower them to achieve their dreams. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Every 4 years we take time out
to marvel at the amazing feats that can be  achieved by the disciplined human athletic
body. New Zealand can take great pride in  every one of our Olympic athletes
representing our country amongst the best in the world, whether they won or were
placed somewhere way down the list. The suc cess of each individual elite athlete in
making the Olympic team represents year s of gruelling physical training, mental
determination, resilience, and, above all, sacrifice by them and their families.
There was disappointment mixed in with gl ory, but this time we did perform above
our weight. According to the  Guardian , which can be relied upon because it is an
English newspaper, per capita of population we  came in fourth. Our congratulations to
4296 Motions 14 Aug 2012
all our medal-winners and members of our Olympic team, and best wishes to the
Paralympians from New Zealand soon to be performing at that theatre in London.
I just want to say something special a bout Valerie Adams and her coach, whose face
told us volumes during and after the event. But even though they suspected something
was seriously wrong, they acted with dignit y, said nothing, and took it like we would
expect a New Zealander to take what l ooked to be an ungracious  circumstance where
they were going to be defeated. Then, of c ourse, we found out the truth, and she is, for
the second time, an Olympic gold medal - winn er. I congratulate her on that and on the
way that she and her coach in particular handled themselves—and, indeed, all our New
Zealanders. But to Valerie Adams, the words of  the great Bard are tr ue: “All’s well that
ends well.”

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātou katoa. I te tuatahi ka mihi r ā ki te Minita, nāna i tuku tētahi pūtea ki te tautoko
i wā tātau tāngata kia haere ki t āwāhi, anā, kua kite mai ai t ātau i ng ā hua i roto o ng ā
Taumāhekeheke o te Ao. In ā tata nei, i rongo au i ng ā Māori e toru, he t āne t ēnei
tokotoru, ko tā rātau kī kua whiwhi i a Te Aitanga-a-M āhaki he mētara koura. Koi nā te

tērā, he mea r ā, ā, ko Ngati Porou t ērā—ka taea e au te eke ki ērā taumata. Koi nei au e
whakanui nei i ēnei k ōrero katoa, ā, me te mihi an ō rā ki ng ā wh ānau i tiaki nei i te
āhuatanga o te w ā kāinga, i a r ātau tāngata i w āhi kē. I kite au i ng ā mea i te pouaka

Me mihi ki te hunga i tiaki nei i ngā momo hākinakina i Aotearoa nei, kia taea e tēnei
hunga te haere ki t āwāhi; ko te hunga i kohi moni nei hai painga m ō ngā mea ka haere

[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings to us all. In the first instance I commend the
Minister for financially supportin g our athletes to enable them  to compete overseas. As
a consequence we have seen the benefits from the Olympic Games. Just recently I

Māhaki had got a gold medal. What was behind that statement? They were celebrating
what Lisa Carrington had done overseas. And so, yes, because their girl had won, they
had won a medal as well. Some might well co nsider, yes, there is a Ngati Porou, a

emphatic: this lass is from the electorate of Waiariki, from Ōhope and Whakatāne.
The circumstances relating to Sarah Walk er have been well and truly documented.
Where is she from? Kawerau and Waiariki. That is that. This person here, Carl
O’Donnell of Rotorua, has har dly had a mention at all. He  has genealogical links to
Tūhoe and Ngāti Awa and is a swimmer. Where is that person from? Waiariki.
The situation relating to soccer and Kristy Hill from within the Ng āti Wh ātua and
Ngāpuhi family tree is correct, but she is real ly from Te Arawa. There are many others
that I must not forget: Karen Hanlen of Ng āti Awa and Te Whakat ōhea. However, I
must leave those stories there, lest I be a ccused by some of hubris through highlighting
outstanding achievements that occur solely in  Waiariki. I must not forget what the
Chiefs and Waikato Bay of Plenty Magic have achieved as well.
The real thrust of my address is to say to the House that it seem s that the Minister’s
entire fund went solely  to Te Waiariki! My response to that is an  absolute no, as that
fund was for the entire country. He distribu ted it to everyone so  that we would all
succeed.
Genealogy is an important thing in Māoridom. As soon as genealogy comes up and a
connection is made a call goes out—that one is  a relation of mine. Regardless of whom
it might be, people take pride in one of thei r own succeeding. It is friendly rivalry and
competition, a cause for good banter, amusement, and entertainment. I must be like that
today, because people take pride in one of  their own succeeding. It is friendly
competition and that is first and foremost.
Secondly, the time has come, shall we say, for young ones in M āoridom to look up at
Māori athletes making it to the top at these leve ls. That, in a nutshell, is the real thrust
of my address. All these athl etes referred to by the majo rity have reached that level

them, yes, they have reached those levels. That is a M āori achieving, that is so-and-so,

back home while their athletes were away at the games. I saw people and some rowers
on television saying that they had not seen their partners for weeks. I sympathise with

I also salute those in New Zealand here who take charge of all sorts of sports, which
enables these athletes to go offshore. I acknowledge the fund-raisers that these athletes
going overseas benefit from, and finally the judges, the timekeepers, and those who look
after the finance and competitors’ needs.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: I have just received a text from Dr
Sharples to say that because of the transl ation service breaking down he would like me
to translate what Mr Flavell has just said. Mr  Flavell has just told the country that most
of those M āori who got medals over at the Olym pic Games were descendants of the
Mātaatua canoe in the first instance. The Mātaatua canoe, as Te Ururoa  and the rest of
Māoridom know, is buried up in Tai Toke rau. So he would like to thank Ng āpuhi for

ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: On the occasion of John Walker’s 40 th
birthday I had the privilege of meeting arguabl y the greatest athlete in the history of the
world. On that occasion I said to Sir Roger Bannister: “Why is it that you have come all
this way to New Zealand to celebrate this  birthday? You’re leaving tomorrow morning
back to London.” He said: “I’ve come around the world to give thanks and praise to one
of the greatest athletes of all time and one of  your great Olympians.” So today we give
thanks and praise to our great Olympians: the young peopl e who have made us proud
these last 2 weeks.
Our success is a remarkable achievement for a small nation. It has promoted our
country centre stage to the rest of the world, with six gold, two silver, and five bronze—
13 medals in all. These medals represent te ns of thousands of hours of commitment and
determination, and much sacrifice. To those who came home victorious, we stand here
today and salute you. In rowing, kayaking, saili ng, and shot-put we showed the rest of
the world that we were truly th e best, and in other sports we  showed that we are a force
to be reckoned with.
The can-do, can-win attitude of the New Z ealand athlete is as time-honoured as that
first 4-minute mile run by Sir Roger Bannister , and the success in London in these past
2 weeks brings much credit to our small country. In one of my  previous roles as
Minister of sport, I attended two Olympic Games—at Atlanta and at Barcelona. There is
nothing like being able to experience the exci tement, privilege, and responsibility of all
the athletes, their coaches, their supporters, and their families firsthand. I am sure Sir
Roger Bannister would be  glad that this Parliament is giving thanks and praise to our
athletes, who have done so well.
On behalf of the ACT Party and all New Zealanders I extend to them all our warmest
congratulations—to those who represented ou r country at these 2012 games in London.
I also extend from the South-west Pacific my  congratulations to Lord Coe. I was with
Lord Coe on the day he was first appointed  to the job of managing the 2012 Olympics.
Britain has done us proud, as the New Zealanders have also done us proud.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I want to join with others in
paying huge tribute to the New Zealand Olympic team for its phenomenal achievements
over the last fortnight. The team not only di d our country proud; it  upheld all of the
Olympic traditions, and it gave a real sense of uplift to this  country in the middle of a
very bleak winter.
We acknowledge and we celebra te our six gold medallists. It is not true, as the
Australians like to gibe, that we do very well in sports where we sit down and go
14 Aug 2012 Motions 4299
backwards! Actually, our rowers, our yachties, our canoeists, and Valerie Adams all did
extraordinarily well and surpassed most peopl e’s reasonable expectations, as did all our
other medallists, and we hung on their every achievement. They deserve our richest and
fullest congratulations. But there were other members of the team who did equally well.
I saw a statistic at the weekend that in th e events New Zealand competed in at the
games, something like three-quarters of our competitors ended up in the top 16 in their
event, and over half of those were in the top eight. So when we make comparisons—and
I think comparisons are probably invidious—ab out where we stand in the international
rankings, I doubt that many countries would ha ve had that level of achievement, with a
significant number of their athletes and thei r performers ending up within the top eight
in the world in their particular events, and winning per capita the number of medals that
we did.
I thank our athletes, our administrators, and everyone associated with the Olympic
performance for the uplift they have given our country in recent weeks, and for the
inspiration that the individual performan ces have given our young people, who now all
see themselves as a Valerie Adams, a Sara h Walker, a Mahe Drysdale, or whomever,
because they have ambition and they have people to look up to. The real achievement of
the Olympic ideal is not just the winning and taking part, not just the being there, not
just the camaraderie, but the inspiration of fu ture generations, and in that our team has
done us exceptionally proud. I thank you all for what you have done, for the sacrifice
you have made, for the dedi cation and the commitment you have shown, and for your
discipline, for your performance, and for your achievement.
Motion agreed to.
Prime Minister—Statements on Charter Schools, Class Sizes, and Dotcom Case
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his recent statements?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that people should not be hung up on
the fact that teachers without  qualifications will be able  to teach New Zealand children
at charter schools?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he also stand by his statem ent: “It’s not the class sizes that
matter; it’s the quality of teaching that we ’re getting in our school s.”, and how can he
guarantee quality of teachers when teachers will not actually need to be qualified?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member knows, the issue of whether teachers are
qualified is being discussed in  the context of charter sc hools, which will offer an
element of choice, although a very small element of choi ce, in the general school
system. All other schools will continue to run with registered teachers.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: When he said, after his U-turn on class sizes: “We have to find
another way to go to lift those teacher qua lity outcomes. And we’ll go away and do
that.”, was having teachers without qualifications what he had in mind?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In respect of the State-run schools, no. In respect of the
charter schools, it is an aspect of provi ding choices for young New Zealanders that are
not currently available to them.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did he read the advice from the Ministry of Education on charter
schools, which said that “There is the challe nge of ensuring that st udents are not put at
4300 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Aug 2012
risk by mentors who are not n ecessarily subject to professional licensing.”; if so, why is
he putting students at risk?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Young New Zealanders are, in those terms, often working
with adults who are not their parents but who are not subject to professional registration

fact, they go on sports trips. They spend a si gnificant, a material, part of their day with

inspiring and motivating our young people.

Cost of Living—Wage Growth and Inflation
2. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What reports has he
received on the cost of living?
14 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4301

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Inflation for the year to June came in
at 1 percent—the lowest rate since 1999. Food pr ices fell 1.8 percent in the year to the
end of July. Fruit and vegetable prices fell 6.6 percent. In th at year the price of grocery
food was down 1.7 percent, and the price of meat and poultry was down 1.6 percent. It
is good to see that inflation is relativel y low. However, many families still have
difficulty meeting their weekly obligations. That is why we are focused on building a
faster-growing economy that supports more jobs and higher incomes.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How do the latest consumer price figures compare with wage
movements in the past year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Although inflation has been falling, the economy has been
growing moderately, and this has been reflec ted in moderate average wage increases.
Annual inflation is running at about 1 percent. The average wage increased by 3 percent
in the past year, or 2 percent more than inflat ion. In addition, floating mortgage rates, at
around 5.75 percent, are at thei r lowest level in almost 50 years. This is giving New
Zealand households a small amount of freeb oard, which they appear to be using to
reduce their debts and increase their savings.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How does the current level of inflation compare with that in

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Inflation is considerably lower now, probably because of the
after-effects of the global financial crisis and a generally more competitive economy.
Annual inflation in November 2008 was running at 5.1 percent. That was made up of 9
years of electricity price increases, whic h added up to 72 percent; floating home
mortgage rates of almost 11 percent; and, of course, the economy having been in a
recession for almost a year. By contrast, th e lower inflation we are now experiencing,
combined with steady increases in average after-tax wages, means that the real spending
power of the average wage earner is increasing slightly.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Over the past 2 years, have or dinary-time wages, as measured
by the Labour Cost Index, grown by 4.24 per cent while prices, as measured by the
Consumers Price Index, have grown by 6.28 percent?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot vouch for exactly thos e figures. What I can tell the
member is that the relationship between th e average ordinary-time wage and inflation
has meant that superannuitants have had a New Zealand superannuation increase in each
of the last 2 years in order to maintain the value of New Zealand superannuation.
Job Creation and Unemployment—Numbers and Government Policy
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : How many New Zealanders are unemployed and
by how many has that number increased si nce the quarter immediat ely before National
came to power in 2008?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): The household labour force survey released last Thursday estimates that
there are 156,400 unemployed. That is a diffe rence of 62,500 from the third quarter of
2008. It is important, of course , to note that one or two th ings have actually occurred
since then: the small matter of the global financial crisis, the fact that we inherited an
economy already in recession before the re st of the world was, and the large
earthquakes in Christchurch. I add those things because I would not want the member to
end up on “Planet Labour” by mistake.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that before National came to power New Zealand had the
eighth-lowest unemployment in the OECD, and it has now slipped to 14 th, why does the
Government claim that New Zealand is doi ng relatively well compared with other
4302 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Aug 2012
developed countries, when, in fact, we are act ually declining relative to other developed
countries?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Again, unfortunately, it appears that the member has taken
a wrong turn and ended up on “Planet Labour”, because the member neglects to note
that the Canterbury earthquakes have had a significant impact on the New Zealand
economy, and that is to be expected. We have  also had the global financial crisis and a
number of other challenges, in fact, including the Psa crisis. Despite that, the economy
has added 77,000 net new jobs  since 2009, and has been st eadily growing despite the
earthquakes and the global financial crisis.

items.text: Why is the Key-Banks Governme nt spending 75 percent of its

transport generates twice as many jobs pe r dollar spent compared with motorway
building, and has much better economic and environmental returns?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The obvious reason would be that people use roads and
they have to be paid to use public transport.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why is the Key-Banks Government fixated on risky deep-sea
drilling as a jobs creation scheme, when mi ning is a very poor job sector—it employs
only 6,000 people—while the Government is neglecting the jobs-ri ch manufacturing
sector, which employs 247,000 New Zealande rs and has shed 25,000 jobs under the
Government’s watch?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member really does need to grow up a little bit. The
reality is—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question did ask why a nd therefore it is seeking the
Minister’s view, but that is not an acceptable way to commence an answer.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I was just pointing out that the member says that the mining
sector is bad for the New Zealand ec onomy, except that if you look at the
unemployment rates by region around Ne w Zealand, you find that the lowest
unemployment rate is in a re gion known as Taranaki, whic h currently has a 3.8 percent
unemployment rate. And if you want to  look across the Tasman, the lowest
unemployment rate is in a state called Western Australia, which happens to be very
focused on mining and resources. So if the me mber wants to say that he is concerned

items.text: Should not a Government that rea lly wants to increase jobs be
fixing the broken monetary policy to give our exporters and domestic manufacturers a

industries that create jobs for New Zealanders rather than profits for foreign investors?

items.text: The member seems to be advocating as his economic
policy New Zealand taking a one-way bet against world currencies. Well, that generally
ends in tears. If the member is actually concerned about jobs—actually concerned about
jobs—he should visit places like Northland, which has the highest unemployment rate,
hold a public meeting, and demand they s upport mining and exploration in Northland.
He should go to Gisborne and tell them to support oil and gas and mineral exploration.
He should support the Exclusive Economic Z one and Continental Shelf (Environmental
Effects) Bill in the House today. He shoul d support the Government building transport
infrastructure, he should support our changes to the emissions trading scheme, and he
should support our efforts to attract—

items.text: Order! The answer is not an opportunity for a speech.

concerned about job opportuni ties for New Zealanders in this country rather than
Australia, he should join the Government in  promoting the opportunities for growth in

Child Poverty, Abuse, and Neglect—Submissions on Green Paper for Vulnerable
Children
5. Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie) to the Minister for

items.speaker: Social Development
items.text: What reports has she received on the public submissions on the
Green Paper for Vulnerable Children  about how to better prot ect our most vulnerable
children from abuse and neglect?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Today we released a
summary of submissions on the Green Paper for Vulnerable Children, and over 600 full
submissions from various organisations. Ther e has been a huge level of public debate
on this. The number of submissions has been impressive, to say the least. At the 17
green paper meetings that I fronted around the country I was just hugely impressed with
people’s willingness to come forward and act ually give their opinions. This process has
resulted in almost 10,000 submissions ma de by non-governmental organisations,
community groups, and members of the publ ic, including over 2,000 from children and
young people.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Why release the submissions summary and the submissions?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Because of transparency. This was a very open and
public consultation process, so I felt it wa s important to releas e as much of this
information as possible. Ideally I would rele ase all of the submissions, but many people
provided very personal information, as they wanted to relate  their own horror stories so
that future children would have better outcomes, and I am going to respect them and
this process.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What was the methodology for analysing the submissions,
and how has it helped drafting the white paper?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: All submissions were given unique identifying numbers.
Various ideas from the submissions were grouped into common categories, and the
frequency with which each idea came up was recorded. This proces s allowed the team
of analysts to describe the submissions’ common ideas and opinions, and indicated how
often submitters raised a particular idea. These submissions are playing a significant
role in the writing of the white paper.

Housing New Zealand Corporation—Time Frames for Maintenance Requests
7. HOLLY WALKER (Green) to the Minister of Housing: What are Housing New
Zealand’s time frames for responding to main tenance requests, and in what percentage
of cases are those timeframes met?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I am advised that response times are
determined by the urgency of work. This is cat egorised in three ways: urgent health and
safety, which needs to be responded to with in 4 hours, and recent results are 93 percent
of jobs completed within that time frame;  urgent responsive ma intenance, which does
not meet the health and safety criteria but is of an urgent natu re, which should be
completed within 2 working days, and recent results are 93 percent of those jobs
completed within the time frame; and gene ral responsive maintenance, which is work
that includes general repairs and must be re sponded to within 10 working days, and 91
percent of those jobs have been completed within the time frame recently. Where work
will take longer to complete, I am advised that the corporation ensures there is no health
and safety risk at the pr operty and, when necessary, su pplies tenants with interim
measures until the work can be completed.

items.speaker: Holly Walker
items.text: Does Housing New Zealand Corpor ation keep records of how many
maintenance requests are outstanding at any given time; if so, how  many are currently
outstanding?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Housing New Zealand Corporation records all maintenance
requests and, clearly, makes a judgment wh ether those are sensible requests and
maintenance does need to be done. Clearly, it measures how many are responded to—in
most cases it is well over 90 percent—so I would imagine it would have a record of
14 Aug 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4307
what requests that have credibility have yet to be responded to. But I must say that not
every request for maintenance is necessarily one that is credible, because sometimes
people would like a couple of garages, some  carports, or whatever , which may not fit
within maintenance criteria.

family sick?

items.text: Can he confirm that urgent health and safety maintenance that should

items.text: As I say, I am not across all 69,000 State house requests,

8. KATRINA SHANKS (National)  to the Minister for Courts : What recent
announcements has he made on the modernisation of our courts system?

items.text: August has already seen two

applications to challenge a fine can be made  online, and last week I announced changes
to allow disputes tribunal applications to be  made online. Last year there were almost
50,000 of these two types of applications, and they were all made in hard copy. Moving
these two applications to th e internet is long overdue, and will save New Zealanders’
time and allow courts to offer a customer-f riendly, cost-effective service that Kiwis
expect.

items.text: What other measures are already in place to make better use of
new technology in the court system?

items.text: These two are just the latest in a long line of
improvements this Government has made to  bring courts into the 21st century. For
example, we have introduced audiovisual links between courts and prisons for many
criminal hearings, saving money and improvi ng public safety, and we are just getting
started with audiovisual links. We have move d to a national model for collecting fines,
which has already cut overdue fines from 48 percent to 44 percent. And we are well on
the way to delivering the electronic opera ting model to courts, which will remove
93,000 hours per year of needless paperwork from  our justice system and allow them to
be reallocated to more proactive work.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: How can he claim that rail safety is being maintained when rotten
sleepers remain in place at critical locations on the rail network?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I think it is worth taking this in context. There are some
7,000 hardwood sleepers that are showing signs of premature decay. That is 0.12
percent of the 6 million - odd sleepers in the network. KiwiRail is taking this very
seriously. It has taken action to test, inspect, and replace the sleepers, and has assured
me and the public that it woul d not run services if  it considered that there was any risk
to public safety.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: How can he claim that rail safety is being maintained when almost
200 KiwiRail maintenance staff are being made redundant despite the backlog of
maintenance, including thousands of rotten railway sleepers not yet replaced?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, because the Turnaround Plan that KiwiRail is
instituting is about business sustainability and putting precious funds to their best
possible uses, but in no way, shape, or form is this compromising safety.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Given the extent of rotten sleepers  at critical leve l crossings, will
he take responsibility for any accidents that occur through a failure of those sleepers?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am not aware of any safety issues where sleepers are
leading to safety issues. Of the two cases  where sleepers that were decaying could
possibly have caused derailments, they were not, as I understand it, near level crossings.
KiwiRail—Financial Targets in Turnaround Plan
12. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister for State Owned

items.speaker: Enterprises
items.text: What advice has he received on th e likelihood of KiwiRail finding $3.85
billion from its own balance sheet as required by the Turnaround Plan?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I am advised there
is little likelihood that KiwiRail will find the $3.85 billion projected in the original 10-

However, it is clear that KiwiRail has a much greater understa nding of its business
drivers, and the company believes it remains on track to meet the original Turnaround

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is he concerned that KiwiRail is laying off 181 workers and deferring

improving the state of the network is the ve ry thing that will allow KiwiRail to reduce
journey times and be more competitive with long-haul trucking?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The board of KiwiRail is determined to achieve the objective
of the Turnaround Plan, it is determined to ma intain safety, and it is determined to run
this business efficiently. Part of that is making sure that its i nvestments are returning
against those objectives, and th at is why it has made the d ecisions it has in respect of
those infrastructure and engineering staff numbers.
4312 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Aug 2012

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Does he support, in the light of the major faults identified in the
Chinese designed and built locomotives, the decision by KiwiRail’s board to not

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Those decisions were manage d by the board of KiwiRail and

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Will he guarantee that the future of the Gisborne to Napier rail line

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The requirement is that there is freight on th e line and in

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No need for that.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he think that the Government’s Turnaround Plan for rail is

we have put $750 million into this projec t, and, frankly, I think the spendaholics
opposite would not be in a position to do anything else.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Hon Nanaia Mahuta seeking to

Overseas Investment Rules—Sale of Crafar Farms

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have also received a letter from  the Hon David Parker seeking to
debate under Standing Order 386 the Governme nt’s decision to approve the sale of
Crafar farms to a foreign purchaser, Milk New Zealand Holdings Ltd. This is a decision
that involves ministerial res ponsibility. Although the decisi on was actually made on 20
April, it was the subject of an appeal. The Court of Appeal has now found that the
Ministers acted reasonably in granting consent for the sale under the Overseas
Investment Act 2005 and dismissed the app eal. The judgment wa s given on 8 August
2012. This is the first time that the matter coul d have come before the House and it is
therefore one of recent occurrence. Given th e significance of the matter, I consider it
important enough to warrant the immediate atte ntion of the House by way of an urgent
debate. I therefore call on the Hon David Parker  to move that the H ouse take note of an
urgent matter of public importance.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I move, That the House take note of a matter of
urgent public importance. The finding of the Court of A ppeal was that the decision was
not unreasonable from a Wednesbury unreasonableness point of  view, not that it was a
reasonable decision. It was that  it was a legal decision, not the right decision. The court
found that the Minister for Land Informati on acted within his powers to approve the
sale of the Crafar farms to  the Shanghai Pengxin syndica te, but not that he acted
reasonably, because that is not its mandate.
I want to talk about what is wrong with this decision. I also want to talk about what is
wrong with the underlying problems in our econ omy that drive the sale of so many of
New Zealand’s assets to overseas people. I also want to put on record some of the
inconsistent statements that we have had from the Prime Minister  and others around
these issues. The Minister approved this sale , the largest ever sale of dairy farmland, on
20 April after his earlier deci sion granting similar approval had been overturned by the
High Court because of misapplication of the le gal test. The largest ever sale of dairy
land to overseas interests is of interest to New Zealanders, and I th ink it is appropriate
that the Speaker—I could not think it inapprop riate, but I agree that it is a matter of
importance that requires the attention of this House.
Why do I say that and what do I say in s upport of that? Well, I would look at our
history in terms of what has happened to our  forestry industry. New Zealand lost large
swathes of its forestry to overseas ownership in a very short period of time—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Approved by you.
4314 Urgent Debates 14 Aug 2012

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Some of them were approved by Labour. Some of them
were approved by Labour. What has happened to the forestry industry since then has
been analysed by people like Brian Gaynor. Brian Gaynor has found that the loss of
control of those assets from New Zealand has led to a smaller portion of the value chain
accruing to New Zealand, because the forest owner who does not have an interest in
New Zealand is less likely to want to process it in New Zealand and less likely to want
to invest in the jobs that add value to New Zealand, and will be more interested in their
own profitability in terms of  maximising the log price. We  in this House should learn
the lessons of history. If we do not learn the lessons of hist ory we are doomed to repeat
them.
Other lessons in history go back a bit further. New Zealand lost a lot of control of the
value from the farming sector in the 19th century when there were high levels—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: The early 19th century.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: —in the early 19 th century when there were high levels of
foreign ownership of New Zealand pastoral  land. As a consequen ce, Governments in
New Zealand tightened up on those rules for the benefit of New Zealand farming, and
that is why we have now got Fonterra, because  we have vertically integrated enterprises
that have as their foundation New Zealand ownership of our land.
Another reason we should be concerned is th at the Prime Minister told us we should
be concerned. The Prime Minister, in the la st term of Government, when there was
public disquiet about the amount of farmland st arting to be sold in to overseas hands,
said he thought that the concerns that New Zealanders had were legitimate. He said that
National would tighten the rules in response to that. Well, what did they do? They
passed this minor change to regulations and pretended it was going to tighten the rules.
The reality is that the discretion of the Mi nister to approve or decline land sales to
foreigners is already very wide. The Mini ster had ample discretion to decline this
application if the Minister wanted to, but he  did not want to. He wanted to approve it
and that is why he did—because it is ministeria l discretion. So when I hear the Minister
claim he had no choice, because it was a departmental recommendation, that is
nonsense. Indeed, if he took the decision on the basis that it was a departmental
recommendation, that would itself be illegal. So when he postures in that way in the
media, he knows he is treading a fine line, because it is ministerial discretion.
This Minister has a record of exercising th at discretion in favour of applications. In
fact, since he has been Minister he has tu rned down only one application, and that was
where the officials found that the applicants were corrupt—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: More than one, is it? How many?

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: About seven.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: About seven now. But it is always on the basis that the
people who are applying are co rrupt individuals rather than the economics of the
underlying transactions.
The second-largest sale ever approved to foreign buyers of dairy land in New
Zealand was also approved by the current Minist er, and that was the sale of a very large
dairy farm on the Maniototo in my home province of Otago. Labour  disapproved of it.
Labour opposed that. We made public our disa pproval of that at the time and we were
not accused of racism for opposing the sale of big dairy farms in  the Maniototo to
American interests—in that case, the Harvard University investment fund.
Prior, the largest ever, in land area and valu e of dairy land, sold to overseas interests
was a Southland group of farms sold to Eu ropean investors. Again, the Labour Party
opposed that. Again, in that case the Labour  Party was not accused of racism for
opposing that particular sale of land to ove rseas buyers. But when we opposed the sale
14 Aug 2012 Urgent Debates 4315
to Shanghai Pengxin the Minister accused us and accused other people of being
motivated by the fact that the purchaser was Chinese, rather than that the purchaser was
of another nationality.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Give us one quote.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: You were on record for that . I am sorry, but the record
shows that the Minister asserted that people were opposed to Shanghai Pengxin
purchasing these farms rather than others on the basis of their nationality, and on the
basis of their ethnicity. That accusation was not made in respect of our opposition to the
US purchase in the second-biggest sale, or  opposition to the European purchase in
Southland earlier.
The opposition of the Labour Party is not based on where people come from. It is
based on what we think is in the long-term economic interests of our country. More than
ever it should be apparent to  the National Party that there are huge trade imbalances in
the world—enormous trade imbalances in th e world. China is running the largest trade
surplus we have ever seen of any country ev er in the history of the world. Germany has
had a trade balance that it has maintained on the back of a euro  that is suppressed
because of problems in the Mediterranean bor der States, which have acted to pull down
the euro and keep up the exports of Germa ny, because they have had a trade advantage
because of their exchange rate.
We have had other countries manipulating their exchange rates. We have these
massive trade imbalances in the world, meaning that countries that ar e in trade deficits
are funding those deficits through borrowi ng more money from overseas and through
selling our assets, which were New Zeala nd - owned, to foreign buyers. Those are the
only two ways you can pay for a current account deficit. Yet we have this Government
ignoring those realities and saying: “Look, we  should just let all of our assets be
available to be purchased by the highest bi dder.” That is just wrong. There is no
economic upside to New Zealand selling th ese land-based assets. We are already the
most efficient farmers in the world. We ar e not going to increase the farm output of
these farms. Indeed, that was one of the r easons why the High C ourt upheld the appeal
in the original decision, which was turned over—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Wrong. You’ve got it wrong.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: It was. One of the reasons was that the High Court was not
convinced that the additional investment that  was going to be made in these farms and
would increase productivity would not have  been made by a New Zealand purchaser.
We know that New Zealand purchasers of fa rms increase productivity. That is how we
have increased our dairy output. That is how Fonterra has thri ved. We do not need
foreign purchasers of those assets to increas e the output of those farms. Indeed, it is
clear that the out put of these farms would have gone  up whoever purchased them, and
New Zealand’s output as a c ountry will not go up as a c onsequence of these farm
purchases.
Even trade access into China is not vastly advantaged through this. We already have
a free-trade agreement with China, which gives us access to that market. So that is not a
huge advantage from these transactions.
The downside is that the future value from our farming sector, if we sell it overseas,
goes to the foreign purchaser. That is a drai n on our resources. Over time we see the
hollowing out of the New Zealand economy. We see this in a rising current account
deficit. A substantial part of our current account deficit is now profit flows, dividends,
interest being paid to overs eas lenders, and profits being re patriated to foreign owners.
We will not get out of this loop with these so rts of policies, because this sort of sale
makes it worse.
4316 Urgent Debates 14 Aug 2012
There are non-economic reasons why we should not be selling these assets. I want to
live in a country where successful New Zeala nders who work hard and save hard can
buy our assets. I do not want al l of our assets priced on an  international market. Some
assets should be priced intern ationally; some should not. I do not want New Zealand to
be a country where a sharemilker who works hard for decades and saves cannot afford
to buy a farm. I do not want the only people who can buy farms in New Zealand to be
people who either inherit large amounts of wealth or bring wealth from overseas.
We are seeing the globalisation of trade. We are seeing the equalisation of prices for
a lot of commodities, and we are seeing the averaging down of a lot of labour costs for
labour-intensive goods, but we are not seeing as set equality. In fact, we are seeing asset
and wealth inequality grow around the worl d. If New Zealand opens itself up to those
forces without protecting our asset base, we do New Zeala nders a disservice. Nowhere
is this clearer than land. You know, we ha ve got countries overseas that for centuries
have had far less egalitarian settings than New Zealand’s. They have had lower rates of
tax. They have had higher rates of division. Ye t the beneficiaries of those settings in
those countries are hugely wealthy compared with New Zealanders. Added to that we
have got the State-based control of enormous  surpluses in some countries, and China is
the obvious example of that. Those two factor s combined mean that we are, unlike any
moment in our history, at risk of overseas people being able to outbid New Zealanders
for our assets, and that is not the sort of c ountry that I want to live in. I do not think it
makes much difference to the economic output  of New Zealand. I do think it increases
our current account deficit over tim e. But it is almost as importa nt to me that I live in a
country where people can afford to own our own country.
This Government should be concentrating on what fixes that problem. It is the
changes that we need to our investment si gnal through a capital gains tax. It is deeper
savings, so that there is more capital to invest in our manufacturing, in our processing of
our forest products, in our fi sheries, and in the high-valu e manufacturing sector. We
need more money in that sector through higher savings, and we need the money directed
there instead of into speculati on. The means to direct it ther e is a capital gains tax to
remove the tax bias that currently puts i nvestment in the wrong place. We need a
research and development tax credit. What we  do not need is to sell ourselves off to
overseas countries for no good reason—no good reason at all.
China does not let us buy its land. Yet we are saying we should have to sell our land
to it. This is wrong. It is not about China; my same logic applies to other countries that
do let us buy their land. I pe rsonally do not think we shoul d sell our rural land to
overseas countries. Neither do I think we s hould sell our infrastructure with monopoly
characteristics. It is really important for the functioning of the—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Why have you changed your view?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: What is that?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Why have you changed your  view, because you sold
off all the—

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Actually, I turned down the sale of Auckland Airport to
Canadian interests, so I will stand on my record. And, actually, I also turned down a
dairy farm at the end of my tenure. The wo rld is changing, and if people cannot change
as the world changes, how moribund would democracy be? We may as well not have it.
I am firmly of the view that  it is not in our interests to sell our rural land, nor our
monopoly infrastructure. It is a symptom of a malaise in New Zealand, which is that we
do not export enough to cover the cost of our imports and interest. Those are the
problems that should be solved. Those are the problems that if solved will raise
incomes, will give job opportunities, and wi ll stop those thousands of New Zealanders
leaving to Australia.
14 Aug 2012 Urgent Debates 4317

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Having the
Labour Party calling for a snap debate on the sa le of land to foreigne rs is really like a
turkey calling for an early Christmas. It is just like mother’s milk for the National Party,
because, frankly, we on this side of the House should be ashamed of our performance
relative to Labour’s. During its time in office,  when David Parker, who has just spoken,
was the Minister for Land Information, over 9 long years that party approved the sale of
665,000 hectares of land to foreigners—665,000 hectares of land to foreigners. Yet
somehow the National Government, which ha s been in power for 3¾ years and has
approved just on 100,000 hectares—that is one-si xth; actually it is more like about a
seventh of what Labour did when it was in  office—is all wrong, evil, disgraceful, and
just outrageous.
How many New Zealanders remember Shan ia Twain buying the South Island high
country estate? Right. How many people re member the then Labour Prime Minister,
Helen Clark, walking the track of the land with Shania Twain and welcoming the
purchase? Right. Let us get some things into perspective here. The total Crafar farmland
area was 7,000 hectares. If anyone wants to get that into persp ective, it is about the size
of a playing card on Eden Park as a percenta ge of total New Zealand land. So when you
sit up in your stand in Eden Park watching the All Blacks play, and you see a little,
white dot somewhere down on the field, and you zoom right in on to it and you find it is
the Queen of Hearts, that is the equivalent piece of Crafar farmland relative to total land
mass. Shania’s Twain’s land was 53,000 hect ares—53,000 hectares was sold to Shania
Twain. Was she a foreigner? Oh well, sh e is from Canada. She now lives in
Switzerland, I think. She split the farm up with he r ex-husband, and he now takes
control of it, or whatever. But Helen Clark walked the track, was absolutely proud of
the Labour Government having so ld this off to Shania Twain, and there were so many
other sales of land that occurred under that party’s administration.
Now it comes time to look at the process. The process was put in place not by the
National Government but by the Labour G overnment. As the Minister for Land
Information I have to work under an Act called the Overseas Investment Act, which was
passed in 2005 by the Labour Government. I am bound to act under that Act. I know
that David Parker wants Ministers to break th e law, but I have got some news for him.
The advice is that if you do not act accordi ngly under the Act and the instructions that
the Act and the regulations give you, you are subject to judicial review, and a buyer
could easily say: “Well, I think the Minister  has breached the intents of the Act and the
regulations.”, take us to judicial review, a nd the courts could easily find that Ministers
have acted outside of it.
David Parker is wrong on a number of count s. First of all, he said that we only
rubber stamp the advice we get. Well, let me give the member a good example. Officials
recommended that the Government say yes to Kim Dotcom’s buying of the Coatesville
mansion. That is the official advice that Mi nisters received, but we  declined it. In a
number of cases, when we did not think th ey were valid buyers of that land, such as
Natural Dairy, when it was wanting to buy it—that is the consortium headed up by May
Wang—we declined it. We said no. But when  my officials brought to me the advice
about the Shanghai Pengxin bid, it is just im possible to go down the list of the criteria
and not be impressed. First of all, what  an incredibly successful company and
companies Shanghai Pengxin is and has run. What a number of various industries,
including retail, construction, and agribusinesses, that comp any has run. When I hear
people like Winston Peters saying: “Oh well, Shanghai Pengxin doesn’t have any
experience of dairy farming.”, well, let us ha ve a look at it. Allan Crafar did, and how
did he go, running the place? OK. He knew ho w to milk a cow. Was it a successful
operation? I am not so sure. I agree that the principal owner of Shanghai Pengxin may
4318 Urgent Debates 14 Aug 2012
not have put on the cups—washed down the udders and put on the cups. I agree with
that. But he has proven that he  has a very successful track record in agribusiness, along
with a number of others.
Then there was the good-character test. In  many cases it is quite easy: you have
someone who has a bit of a dodgy background  or who has convictions, or whatever.
This was a clean slate—a clean slate for a good-character test. So you could not do it on
that. Then we get to the economic acumen. In  the past, and I want members to really
focus on this, Ministers, since the Act was put in place, have always used the “before
and after” test—that is, what would be the value of this asset before the investment was
made, and what will be the value of this asse t after? That is the test that David Parker
used over and over again, because I have check ed with the officials who were the same
officials who worked under Labour. We alwa ys use the “before and after” test. But
somehow, a High Court judge told us we we re wrong. Justice Forrest  Miller said: “No.
Ministers have misdirected themselves and should not use a ‘before and after’ test. They
should use a ‘with and without’ test.” They should ask what is th e value of the asset
with this investment, and what  would be the value of this asset without the investment
being made?”. It is quite difficult to do, because the “without” is billions of
combinatorics. Who knows what would happe n to the asset without the investment?
Who knows? It could be the best dairy farmer  the world has ever seen who buys it, and
it might be the most flourishing  set of farms ever, or it mi ght be another Allan Crafar
who buys it, or anything in between. But we took the advice of the High Court. We
went back and we applied the “with and w ithout” test. After being challenged again in
the Court of Appeal, I am delighted to sa y the Court of Appeal  found in favour, that
Ministers had acted properly, and had approved the sale under the Act.
Let us get it quite clear. This Act was put in place by Labour, so you cannot start
blaming the National Government for the Ac t, and, indeed, you cannot even blame the
National Government for the regulations in  place, because National added some more.
We did not delete any; we left all the regulations that are under the Overseas Investment
Act in place, and added two new ones, afte r we did a review. One was an economic
interest test—factors allowing Ministers to  consider whether New Zealand’s economic
interests are adequately safeguarded and pr omoted. That was the first extra test we
added. A second one was a new mitigating factor  that enables the Minister to consider
whether an overseas investment provides opportunities for New Z ealand oversight or
involvement. Well, this one does. This is goi ng to be a joint partnership with Landcorp.
Landcorp is going to have a lot of its expertise involved in that.
Now I get to the point that I find really laughable. We are supposedly now selling off
all our country. You listen to Russel Norman  from the Greens, who himself has come
here only recently from Australia,  so I find it a bit rich that  he is saying we do not want
foreigners to take over our land. But you lis ten to Russel Norman and you would think
that the vast bulk of this country now lies in the hands of forei gners. I can do nothing
but thank the Sunday Star-Times because it did a fantastic, big exposé of this a couple of
weeks ago, in July, in which it showed a huge piece of the pie. It asked how much land
foreigners are gobbling up. Most people say that it is most of our country. We are
becoming tenants in our own land. It is all going.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: That was the Prime Minister who said that.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, the Prime Minister sa id he did not want to
be a tenant in his own land, so let us ge t the facts right. All that the Terralink
