not about anything except money. Treasury wrot e the book and said: “Let’s have a plan
to actually make this affordable. Let’s cu t back on education. Let’s pretend it’s an
investment.” But Treasury c ould not convince the rest of  the country. It had the
Government on its side, but nobody else—nobody else. So we saw fantastic unity across
a sector that is not always unified and does not always speak with one voice, and the
Government was forced to do a back-down. We ll, that is an indication not that it had
learnt, and not that it believed that the parents were right, but that it had realised it could
not sell the policy. This was a cynical and depressing scenario, because we asked the
Minister whether she had changed her view af ter hearing from parents, and she said she
had not. She still thought it was a great idea, and it is very, very sad for the parents and
children of New Zealand that that was the agenda.
Some information on national standards was put on the website last week, and, again,
it is a real mess. It is a real cut a nd paste job. You cannot understand what you are
reading, you do not know what it is that  you are going to get—sorry, not you, Mr
Chair—what the parents will get, and it does not make any sense. The moderation tool
that is being developed at great expense—about $5 million has been spent so far on
developing the work around national standards,  but it is not finished—will not be ready
until 2014. So what are people go ing to make of that? The Government put up a policy
that had no tool for creating any kind of moderation, and although it will not be on offer
until 2014, somehow the parents are going to get the benefit of reading the data, which
are completely different from school to school. That is somehow supposed to be
softening the parents up for the standards.  Even if you believed that was a good idea, it
is a bad way to have gone about it.
The Green Party does not think that league  tables are a good id ea. We think that
league tables are for sports teams. League ta bles are great in the Olympics, but they are
not for children. Labels are useful on jam jars, but not on children. Our fundamental
problem with national standards is not the way that they are being delivered but the idea
that a narrow mechanism that reduces the New Zealand curriculum—which is upheld
around the world as a valuable and broad cu rriculum—to a narrow set of literacy and
numeracy standards is narrowing teachers’ re quirements to teach to the test. No matter
what the Government says, there is huge anxiety out there.
It would be interest ing if people listened to the evidence of people like Professor
Martin Thrupp, who went to England and looked at the model over there. Some
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4339
countries have gone around the track, and they have followed the track of increasingly
narrowing and teaching to the test—Britain is one of th em. Others—for example,
Finland and some of the Asian countri es—have gone the opposite way and have
invested in a broad curriculum. The results are very clear. Britain and the United States
are failing the children who are already struggling because of poverty and social
context. Initiatives like na tional standards only create an xiety, and they are driving
teachers out of the profession, because people become teachers from the sense of moral
mission to have an input into children’s liv es. Children need the best people in this
country, but the best people will be driven out if we narrow what has been established
as being an excellent curriculum and turn it into a bunch of mechanisms.
It is lovely to read numbers; they make  life really simple. But guess what! Numbers
do not reflect the reality of what the comp lex matter of each child ’s individual learning
is actually about. I wonder whether the Gove rnment actually looked at what learning
means instead of what numbers mean when  it set up these standards, because the
standards are absolutely incapable of deliver ing rich and contextual—which is what the
Minister calls it—information for parents. It is a sad si ght when you see this being
justified on a daily basis in this House. It is not what people voted for, at all. They voted
for the idea of our kids all doing well. What they got was this mechanistic, failed
system, which is incoherent and has not ev en been properly moderated. Quite frankly,
that, along with class sizes and charter schools, is an unmitigated disaster.
What is also a disaster is the lack of c oherence in the Government’s way of relating
to the sector. You cannot improve child ren’s learning unle ss you have good
relationships not only with child and teacher but  also with teachers and politicians. I am
not saying the teachers always get it right, but what I am sayi ng is that declaring war on
the education sector, the academics, and the professionals is not the way in which you
make change happen. We all agree that there are kids who need more support in school.
And some of us know that that is because  the goal of the school system should be
equity. The Finns are at the top of the Programme for Inte rnational Student Assessment
table because the goal of their education syst em is not achievement; it is equity. Equity
comes first, then participation, and then achievement.
But why listen to the experts? After all,  the Finns have many good models that we
would do better to look at than  looking at Britain and the United States, where we have
these bizarre failures. Look at Florida. Hurricane Katrina has turned into an educational
disaster. What happened is that public schooli ng collapsed. Because of the disaster they
have brought in these experime ntal charter schools—these for-profits—and as a result
you have children falling through the cracks in greater numbers than ever before. That is
a tragedy.
We must make sure that we do not le t what has been a good education system
become a game for Treasury, an experiment for the Government, and a sacrifice of the
good things, under the fake mythology that what we need is running schools like a
business. What we need is to run educati on like it is for liberation, for life, and for
lifelong learning. It is not a mechanistic busin ess. It is a mission. We should take on the
Finns’ ideal, which is that not everybody can be a teacher. They invest a huge amount in
teacher training. They say that if you want to  lift the quality of the education system,
you must lift the quality of the people who are allowed to be teachers. So instead of
saying the most fabulous job you can have is to be a corpor ate financial speculator, or
some kind of merchant banker, or  that being a lawyer or even an MP is the best job in
the world, the best job in the world needs to be a teacher. Then we will get the quality of
teaching—

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak on the
Appropriations (2012/13 Estimates) Bill. I want to acknowledge the Minister of
4340 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Education, Hekia Parata, because I think she ha s a plan for education in this country,
unlike the Opposition.
I want to start by talking about the increa sed investment in education. Under our
Government this is the fourth successive Budget whereby we have  increased education
funding. We are now spending $9.6 billion in this country; $500 million more in the last
Budget. Can I also say that I think a very clear ideological point has been made by the
Opposition today. Today the Opposition has said that, basically, parents have no role in
students’ learning, but ev ery single night when pa rents read to their children when they
get home, they are involved in the learning pathway. When you look at this Budget, and
when you look at the initiatives that we have put forward—whether it is national
standards and providing greater data to pare nts, whether it is gr eater accountability and
choice within our education system—you will s ee that we believe on this side of the
House that it is not OK that one in five ch ildren leave our education system not being
able to read and write properly. What we are focused on is accepting that there are some
amazing teachers and principals in this country, but the literacy rate is not an acceptable
standard for this country. That is why you ha ve seen in this Budge t, firstly, a massive
increase in what we are spending, and sec ondly, some targeted in itiatives, which are
focused on those children, and I want to talk about a couple of those.
The first thing is that when it comes to early childhood education, we are seeing a
massive funding increase—a 34 percent incr ease since 2008. That is  huge, and it is
particularly focused on M āori and Pasifika kids. We have seen $47 million in targeted
initiatives to ensure that M āori and Pasifika kids are not on the back foot when they
start out in our educa tion system. We have also put forw ard the initiative of partnership
schools. What that is about is saying that for some students a different model may work.
We have seen huge interest from iwi, and from Pasifika organisations, and I want to
give people an example of that. At my se lect committee, the Education and Science
Committee, we currently have an inquiry into Pacific languages. I want members
opposite to think about this for a moment. There are many Pasifika students who have
barriers to our education system in the area of language. I want members opposite to
think about certain schools having a system where some of those teachers, or some of
the other people who come into those sc hools, have a speciality in language and
whether that would actually help a number of Pasifika students. So from my perspective
this is about greater choice and about provid ing for some of those most disadvantaged
students another option.
The other big aspect of our education plan is lifting achievement. What we are saying
on this side of the House is that the status  quo is not acceptable. That is why we have
implemented national standards, because, agai n, we believe that pare nts have a right to
certain data about how thei r children are doing so that they can be involved in a
student’s pathway in terms of their lear ning. So there is a philosophical and an
ideological difference between members on th e opposite side and our members. We do
value the role of teachers and principals in th is country, but we also believe that parents
have a key role to play in learning. That  is why, when we have put forward national
standards, we have actually said: “Look, we’re not interested in league tables, but we
are interested in providing good data to parents about how their students are doing.” We
also believe that the other aspect  of our education plan is a 21 st century education
system. That is why we have put $1.5 billion into ultra-fa st broadband. That is why, as
part of the mixed-ownership model that has been opposed by members opposite, we are
putting a billion dollars into modernising schools.
So what you can see here, on th is side of the Chamber, is a very clear education plan
that has increased investment in edu cation—$500 million in this Budget—that has
greater transparency and accountability through national standards, and that has targeted
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4341
initiatives to particularly vulnerable student s, whether it is the $47 million in terms of
early childhood education, whethe r it is partnership schools, wh ether it is ensuring that
we actually have decent data about where these kids—some of these kids who are
failing—are, or whether it is th e Youth Guarantee pl aces that we have  put forward. We
have been very focused on saying that  although P ākehā kids second in the world, for
Māori and Pasifika kids , I think, it is 33 rd and 44 th respectively, and we cannot have a
situation where the status quo remains. Me mbers opposite have demonstrated they are
living in a 1950s world, where they believe th at on an ideological basis teachers are the
only people who can be involved in learning.  We do not believe that, and that is
reflected in an increased budget, targeted in itiatives for some of our most vulnerable,
and increased transparency—

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Kia ora
tātou katoa. Last week there was the Inte rnational Day of the World’s Indigenous
Peoples, which probably passed most of us by, so I want to reflect in my contribution to
this debate on a statement out of the Decl aration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. I
am talking about article 14, which states th at “Indigenous peoples have the right to
establish and control their educational syst ems and institutions providing education in
their own languages, in a manne r appropriate to their cultu ral methods of teaching and
learning.”, and that we “have the right to al l levels and forms of education … without
discrimination.”
So you would understand that against that  background, and with Pita Sharples as
Associate Minister of Education, we are relatively comfortable and actually quite happy
with the amount of money we are able to secure in resp ect of advancing M āori
education. What I am talking about is a coup le of areas in Budget 2012. Firstly, there is
$76 million specifically targeted at Māori education. There is a particular focus on early
childhood education, with an emphasis on Te Reo M āori and tikanga M āori—$35
million all up. In another area it is targeting resources, $8.5 million, to support learners
to achieve National Certificate of Educa tional Achievement—in particular, in M āori-
medium education. Finally, the other procurement we got was a massive $33 million for
teaching, leadership, and curriculum focus to accelerate the achievement of M āori
learners.
That is all pretty fantastic from our point of view—in particular, from a M āori Party
perspective and being in an agreement w ith the National Government—because these
gains are for our wh ānau through education. But I do wa nt to sound one particular
warning, and it is specifically focused on the 95 percent of young M āori students who
are in a general-stream school. Education of  our tamariki in those mainstream schools
we believe is very much a priority that we  should pretty much focus on. Of course, the
Minister of Education, Hekia Parata, ha s been upfront, I suggest, about demanding
excellence and requiring accountability, and in some forums has actually copped a lot of
flak for her particular stand. From my perspective, her intentions, I think, are
honourable. But we need to see the difference. We need to see the difference that it is
going to make in terms of young Māori learners.
One of the things that the M āori Party did try to advance is a kaupapa called
Tātaiako, which is all about cultural competency and setting some standards for teachers
to achieve that they need to develop in order to engage M āori learners to achieve at the
very highest level. It has not been rolled a ll the way out as yet, but we are hoping that it
will achieve that. The key point about T ātaiako is that it was developed to help all
educators think about what it takes to successfully teach M āori learners. It is not a
responsibility that any educator, we beli eve, should shirk or refer on to the M āori
teachers to deliver. We expect that action a nd accountability must come from all of our
educators. We must see action, because for far too long we have been talking about a lot
4342 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
of initiatives without too much movement in  respect of achievement levels. Too many
staff in schools, I believe, have got Ka Hik itia in their right hands, but have wrapped it
up in cellophane and it has never been opened. Although we might have the strategy, we
actually have not moved towards implementing it in a strong way to address the
kaupapa of Ka Hikitia at its very heart.
If the Education Review Office is charged with holding schools to account, then we
would expect to see it have much more transparency around the schools that deliver and
the schools that are clearly failing to make  a difference. We must do that. Although
there is a mechanism within the Edu cation Review Office, an accountability
mechanism, it sort of stops there, because nothing is taken on. The Promoting Success
for M āori Students: Schools’ Progress  study, which was recently published, surveyed
287 schools, from full primary to secondary sc hool level, and the data showed clearly
that sustained M āori underachievement was basically a part of our education system.
The report found that a substantial numbe r of schools did not review their own
performance in relation to M āori achievement, did not make e ffective use of the data to
improve programmes, and did not conduct rese arch about students’ learning. Is it that
they do not really care, or is it that they ju st do not know what to do? Well, whatever it
is, it is not good enough, and from our perspective, from the M āori Party perspective,
we need to do it far better. I suppose that is why—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Just before I call the next member, the
Māori Party has used its allocation. If the memb er wishes to take other calls, they will
have to talk to one of the other parties.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: In this debate about th e budget for education, the
National Government contribution is that it would have you believe that what it is
concerned about is children who are not ach ieving. That is what those members have
said the problem definition is. How come John Key’s solution was to increase class
sizes? How on earth could increased class sizes  actually help children to achieve better
in terms of their education? It is just a ridiculous proposition. The New Zealand public
smelt it from a mile away. They did not need  official advice. They did not need the
spin-doctoring. They understood, and New Zeala nd parents especially got this straight
away. It was an absolute nonsense for that G overnment to try to pr etend that increasing
class sizes was somehow going to improve education and somehow going to have those
children who are not achieving in educa tion now suddenly achieving. Well, it was a
complete nonsense and everyone knows it. Everyone now knows that that Government
does not know what it is doing with regard to education.
They also know that it is not a priority for this Government. The Government cannot
put that genie back in the bottle, because even though it backed down because of the
pressure that came on from parents, every pa rent in New Zealand now knows that that
Government believes that increasing class sizes is the thing to  do to improve our
children’s education. Well, the Government got it badly wrong, and it got it so badly
wrong that New Zealand families now know that this Government is out of touch with
their aims and aspirations. The sorts of aspirations that New Zealand families have are
for better quality education.
I want to focus on early childhood education because that is where it started with this
Government. This Government cut the fundi ng back in 2010 to qualified staff in the
early childhood education sector.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: Remember your maths!

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That is exactly where it started from. Louise Upston is
pretending that it did not, but the Budget documents show $400 million worth of money
cut from early childhood education, from qua lified staff. It was the funding bands for
qualified staff that actually were the first vi ctim of this Government. It happened in
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4343
early childhood education, but it is not going to stop there,  because that was just the
beginning of that Government saying that  it does not believe in having qualified
teachers in education. It fundamentally does not believe that. The Government got away
with it in early childhood e ducation, and now it is putting  that into our compulsory
education sector via the Trojan Horse of  charter schools—but it did start in early
childhood education.
It has got even worse for early childhood education in this current Budget that we are
debating here today. The Government has not  inflation-adjusted the fees for early
childhood education. What is that going to mean? It is going to mean that fees are going
to increase for families. Parents are going to pay all over again because of that
Government’s folly, and because the Government cannot see how important quality
early childhood education is to New Zealand families. The Government was warned
about this; it was given official advice about this. It was told by the ministry that—and I
am going to quote now from Budget documents th at have been released recently by the
ministry—“Not providing a unive rsal cost adjustment may lead to providers taking a
further opportunity to increase fees. These fee increases decrease the affordability of
ECE for families, with the largest impact on priority groups.” By “priority groups” what
it meant was M āori, Pacific Island, and low-income families. The official advice was
that this year’s Budget would actually advers ely impact on that very group. So I do not
want to hear any more from that side of the Chamber, from the Government, getting up
and pretending that that is where it is putting its energy and its efforts, because the
official advice actually shows it up for wh at it is. The official advice is that not
inflation-proofing fees for early childhood education will impact on those very groups.
But that is after those groups have alread y had an 11 percent increase in their costs
for early childhood education in just 2011 al one. This is a cumulative effect for
families. They have already had a cost  increase by the Government—not by the
recession, not by any other mechanism than a decision of that National Government.
The fees for early childhood education increa sed by an average of 11 percent. Now the
Government is going to increase them by more , with this year’s B udget. An average of
11 percent, by the way, means that some families are paying 25 percent more, and some
families are not.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Education Review Office agreed to.
Vote Pacific Island Affairs agreed to.
Vote Arts, Culture and Heritage agreed to.
Vote Attorney-General agreed to.
Vote Parliamentary Counsel agreed to.
Vote Treaty Negotiations agreed to.
Vote Social Development

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Thank you for the
opportunity to take a call on th e estimates for Vote Social Development. There is no
doubt about it that this is a big year for so cial development. If you look across what we
are doing as far as the progression and the wo rk in this portfoli o, you cannot go further
than, I think, three main areas of work, a nd probably counting from there. The main
areas would certainly be in welfare reform. We have already seen welfare reform phase
one go through. They would certainly be around the white paper and the changes within
4344 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Child, Youth and Family and the developments there, and also investing in services for
outcomes, which relates to changes in how we are contracting with NGOs, in particular,
but also, I think, wider than that, in the work that we are doing in communities.
Added to that, of course, is  the work that we are doing with youth, which has been a
huge focus for us, and, along with the Associat e Ministers in this portfolio, we have
made a substantial difference. I know that  Minister Borrows, with his Associate
Minister hat on, would take th e opportunity to talk a lo t about youth offending and the
progress that we have seen there in the ch anges to not just sentencing, I think, but,
more, the preventive work that is being done  in community organisations and with the
police as well. That investment, which we ma de years ago, is certainly paying off, but I
will leave that to him.
I thought it was opportune, because we have certainly had questions around it today.
Today we released the summary of the green paper and the submissions that were made
on that in the writing of the wh ite paper. So it is an opport une time to sort of look at
where we are at and what we are doing when  it comes to Child, Youth and Family and
the notifications there. On  average, at the moment we are getting around 150,000 to
155,000 notifications, of which around 55,000 are deemed to need follow-up. And from
there we have about 22,000 substantiated cases  of abuse or neglec t. When you look at
the figures in the areas of physical abus e and sexual abuse, they are not actually
increasing. They have been fairly stable, if you like, over a long period of time in this
country. Where you see a huge increase is in emotional abuse and how that is
categorised. So in one respect you can sort of say that it is horrifi c that any level of
abuse is going up, but I think if you looked at it from a different angle you would say
that at least we are identifyi ng it now as what it is and, in many cases, taking it a bit
more seriously. That was under Labour, quite frankly, so I am not standing here to say
that that has particularly changed there. What we have seen is most certainly an
increase, and then changes in how we approach it.
Differential response within Child, Youth and Family is making a big difference.
You see that in the estimates, as to where we  put that kind of funding. That is where we
have community organisations dealing with the lower levels of abuse and neglect of
these children, and that makes a difference. Community organisations are, at times, able
to get into people’s homes differently from, quite frankly, how social workers or police
can. They can work with them in a different way and, at times, get different results from
perhaps that social worker, who is seen as being statutory. That does not mean, of
course, that social workers are not stepping in and, unfortunately, doing far too much of
their share of this work—hence why we ha ve put 96 more social workers in: 16
supervisors, with 80 more. Fifty-seven have now been appointed, which I am absolutely
thrilled about. They are in positions, training up, and getting to know the system.
What we also need to do is look carefu lly at whom Child, Youth and Family is
working with. I know that the Opposition has e xpressed interest in this, and I think it
really is an area that we are constantly l ooking at—whether there is any filtering done
by police, for example, who make up someth ing like, from memory, 76 percent of the
notifications that are coming through. At the moment, if there is a child in the house—
they do not even need to witness violen ce or anything else—the police pass that
notification directly on to Child, Youth and Family. We need to actually have that
discussion and that debate as to whether or not there should be a little more filtering
done at the police end, because, at the end of the day, you have social workers then
spreading themselves across the board, and perhaps working on cases that they do not
need to, and, as a consequence, you get a number of false positives.
Certainly, what you see coming out of subm issions is the debate around targeting.
You have universal services that cross acro ss health, education, and, of course, social
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4345
development, but, equally, you then need to l ook at whom you are targeting. So if there
is anything in that work that you are doing within Child, Youth and Family to prevent
some of these children from being abused and neglected, it is looking at who they are
and where they are, and then working it out and making sure we ha ve got the absolute
right service delivery from the right professionals around them.
This is a substantial portf olio—you could say with a subs tantial Minister, I suppose,
if you had a sense of humour—so what it needs is that concerted vision and approach to
it from all directions—

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I appreciate the Minister for Social Development
outlining for us some of the reasons behind the dramatic increase in child protection
notifications that we have seen in recent times—and they are dramatic. I know she
acknowledges that and the different reasons for that, but I still have grave concerns over
the workload that our Child, Youth and Fa mily and our front-line social workers
currently have and whether or not, in essenc e, 50 new social workers is enough to deal
with the massive demand that we have.
It is timely that we are here in this Cham ber discussing the state of children given
that the summary of submissions on vulne rable children was released today. I look
forward to responding to that in further de tail—it looks like you are about to interrupt
me, Mr Chair, for the dinner break—when we come back—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. The time has, in fact, come for me to leave the Chair.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Kia ora t ātou, nō reira, tēnā koutou,
tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. Honourable members, the House is in Committee on the
Appropriation (2012/2013 Estimates) Bill, and it is resumed. Before the dinner break,
the honourable member Jacinda Ardern wa s speaking and addressing the Committee.
She was debating Vote Social Development and she has 4 minutes remaining if she
wishes to seek the call.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I wa s indeed addressing the
Committee before the dinner break, and I do want to come back to the issue I was
touching on, which was introduced by the Minist er in the chair, the Hon Paula Bennett,
and that was the issue of vul nerable children and the release today of the summary of
submissions on the Green Paper for Vulnerable Children. There has been an
overwhelming response, I think it is fair to say, to the Green Paper for Vulnerable
Children. Thousands of people have responded to the call on what it is that the
Government should do in response to th e issue of children’s  well-being in New
Zealand.
I applaud all those who took the time to be  a part of that discussion. Contained in
those submissions are themes that I wa nt to touch on. One was the issue of
universalism. It was the Mini ster herself who asked whethe r we should start targeting
services in a more concentrated fashion to wards those children whom we, the State,
consider to be at risk. An overwhelming me ssage from submitters was that we need to
exercise caution in doing so, because, in fact , even the notion of vulnerability is very
fraught. All children, by default almost, ar e vulnerable by their very nature. So
narrowing the targeting of services is a fraught business and we need to exercise caution
there.
Submitters also raised the issue of bipartisanship. They want parties to work
together. The primary reason for that, I th ink, was to see enduri ng solutions around
child poverty and children’s well-being genera lly. That is something on which I, as
Labour’s spokesperson on social developmen t, again extend the offer that Labour
4346 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
extended when Annette King was our spokesp erson—that we are happy to work with
this Government on issues relating to ch ildren’s well-being. But I do so with the one
disclaimer: we think the bar needs to be raised.
The green paper highlighted the issues that  the National Government wants to focus
on when it comes to what it perceives to be  vulnerable children: information sharing,
mandatory reporting, and the way the agencies are engaging with families. Our
contention has been that we need to take a much broader approach when it comes to the
well-being of children. We need to look at issues like income adequacy, poverty,
housing, health, and education. Th ese are all things that we know have an impact on
children’s well-being or otherw ise, and to ignore those and simply hone in, in the way
that this Government has, is at our peril an d to the detriment of our children. In fact, we
pay for it down the track.
If I were to pick out one issue in particular  that the Labour Party, as part of its core
fundamental values on fairness and social ju stice is concerned about, it is the issue of
child poverty. I asked the Minister in questi on time today a very simple question: “How
many children in New Zealand are currently living in poverty?”. Th e answer was that
we do not have an official measure in Ne w Zealand. If Unicef is able to produce a
scorecard by which it measures every OECD nation on what it considers to be a fair and
reasonable measure of child poverty, surely this Government—if it claims that poverty
is a priority issue—would have at least an interest in knowing how many children in this
country are living in poverty. But the message that we got back from the Minister today
was that knowing how many children are in poverty is not a priority.
If she does not want to know how many ch ildren are living in poverty, how is she
possibly concerned with even getting them out  of that situation? Forgive my cynicism,
but if this Government is unwilling to at leas t put a figure on this i ssue, or even try, we
are never going to at least see a target around the 270,000 children living in poverty.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Malo soifua. I want to first
congratulate the Minister in the chair, the Minister for Social Development, on the great
work that she and the Social Services Committee have done to bring the first welfare
reforms to this House, and we certainly look forward to our second phase of welfare
reforms, to be coming up in the next couple of months.
I also want to thank th e previous speaker, Jacinda  Ardern, too. I found her
contributions thoughtful and cons istent, and only a little misguided. In referring to
Child, Youth and Family’s performance over the last few years, before the dinner break,
she mentioned the number of unallocated cas es and how unacceptable that was. Well,
what Miss Ardern did not mention was th at the number of unallocated cases was
reduced by 93 percent between 2006 and 2011. Mr Cunliffe might smile, having been
on holiday in the northern hemisphere, but that means that 1,089 cases in 2006 went
down to 71 cases in 2011. As at March 2012 there were 41 un allocated cases, including
one critical. A safety assessment is completed within 24 hours by the duty social worker
for all critical unallocated cases. Child, Y outh and Family have met or exceeded 96
percent of their targets, in cluding notification response-time targets in 2010-11—that is
right, 96 percent of targets.  And, guess what? In 2009-10, Mr Cunliffe, it exceeded 100
percent—100 percent. That  is compared with 55 pe rcent under Mr Cunliffe’s
Government.
The final point I would like to raise to Miss  Ardern’s assertions before the dinner
break is to make it quite clear in public that that member, along with her then high-
performing Minister Ms Dyson, along with the deputy leader, Grant Robertson, and
along with the chief whip w ho sits here today, Mr Hipki ns, were all working on the
ninth floor at that time, and they were dir ectly responsible for some of those figures
being so poor in 2006. Miss Ardern says that th e bar needs to be lifted. Well, I say that
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4347
it has been lifted by 93 percent. Read the figures, go to Statistics New Zealand, and you
will see where the problem is.
So what is the problem? Well, we all know what the problems are, but the Labour

items.speaker: Opposition may not know
items.text: 13 percent of our working-aged population is on a benefit,
and 200,000 Kiwi kids are growing up in bene fit-dependent homes. That is a life of
limited choices and outcomes. I could talk about the other problems that we have—how
David Shearer bashes benefici ary fraudsters, unlike Miss Ardern, of course. But that
would be remiss of me, because it does not  need a backbench National MP to show
what a shambles that Opposition is in.
So what are we doing? What are we doing? The reason our Government has the trust
of the New Zealand public is that we are fo cused on the issues that actually matter to
New Zealanders—the economy, jobs, and oppor tunities, as well as education and
health. That is right. In Budget 2012 we are providing an  upfront investment of over
$287 million over the next 4 years in the first phase of these welfare reforms. We have
always said that welfare reform would cost  more up front, because in order to spend
more up front and save more in the long term , that translates to more support to help
people off welfare and into work.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Not very convincing, Sam.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: The Labour Party does not lik e that. Sue Moroney does
not like that at all—th e fact that we are helping the vulnerable out of poverty and off
benefits and into work. Phase one of th at funding includes $81.5 million of additional
money over and above what has been sent in the last financial year. The second phase of
the reforms, of course, will be funded in Budget 2013.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Who will that deal to?

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: The entire welfare package is expected to cost at least
$520 million, Ms Moroney, and it is expected to save, in the long term, $1 billion. That
is a net saving of $480 million, and Labour does not like it.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Nobody believes it.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Unlike you, we believe in investing in our youth. We
believe in investing in our early childhood educ ation system. We believe in investing in
mentoring, parenting, and budgeting courses.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in this debate on Vote Social
Development. I think my contribution will me sh nicely with that of the Minister for
Social Development and of Ms Ardern; I am not so sure that it will mesh all that nicely
with Sam Lotu-Iiga’s contribution. The Minist er referred to the publication today of the
summary of submissions on the green paper. I want to take that as my starting point,
because while we have had this consultati on with the public around the Green Paper for
Vulnerable Children, we have also had the M āori Affairs Committee considering what
needs to be done for M āori children, and I sit on the Health Committee, which is
engaged in an inquiry into  practical steps for improvi ng child health outcomes and
reducing child abuse. Many of the submitters to those three processes have been
expressing some degree of be wilderment and, sometimes, frus tration about the fact that
there are three processes. I th ink what this amounts to is th at actually for people in the
community, their lives are being lived in an entirely unsiloed way, whereas our response
as a Parliament, and the State’s response to people’s needs, is instead fragmented and
broken into silos. I guess those three inquiries are emblematic of exactly that issue.
What we have is a situation where the challenges that people face are not well met by
that fragmented response by the State. What we need to do is to find ways of working
across silos—working in a cross-sectoral way—to address the needs that people have. It
is no surprise at all to anyone working in any of those three areas, including the area
that we are looking at now of social development, that the families and the communities
4348 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
who have the greatest needs in the social development area are the very same ones who
have the greatest needs in health, or, indeed, in housing or in education. We need to find
a way of addressing problems that will a ddress those heart problems, because those
communities are typically M āori communities, Pasifika communities, poor
communities, or communities ma rginalised in some other way. So those issues are the
ones that we need to address.
In the area that I know best, in health, th at problem, which we are facing in social
development and in those ot her sectors, is an increas ing problem. The gaps, the
inequalities in outcomes, and the way in which inequalities drive worse outcomes—in
both the causes and the effects—those pr oblems are becoming worse. We are seeing
worse health outcomes for the poorest and the most marginalised, and the same is the
case in those other sectors. It is an increas ing problem, and one that we need to deal
with.
In years gone by, I worked across sectors tryi ng to get cross-sectoral collaboration.
Although there was generally agreement th at this was a good thing to do, it was
typically a very hard thing to have happen, because nobody had the resources to make it
happen. If I can now just give some praise to the last Labour Government—in its very
last term of Government, it actually changed that. The Ministry of Social Development
had, for the first time, the manda te to facilitate and fund cross-sector al collaboration. I
believe that if there is an opportunity that arises from having these parallel inquiries and
these parallel processes going on, it must be this: to again find a way of making cross-
sectoral collaboration actually happen on the ground.
I acknowledge the Minister’s recognition of the value of cross-party collaboration. I
recognise Jacinda Ardern’s call for that same  thing. I suggest to the Government that
here is a great opportunity to make somethi ng of these inquiries, and to call on other
parties to collaborate.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Ahn nyung ha se yo. It is a great pleasure to rise to take
a call in this estimates debate. I would lik e to echo my chairperson of the Social
Services Committee, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, and his acknowledgment of the Minister for
Social Development, because I have seen th e passion in her eyes when she talks about
welfare. She would be unriv alled in her passion and her hard work. I would like to
thank her, to start off with.
Is it not interesting to hear Mr Hague ta lking about the imbalance in society? The
members opposite have actually opposed ever y single growth initiative we have
proposed, just as they have opposed every single restraint that we have made to get back
into surplus, just as they have said no to  making welfare work in this country, yet they
still talk about inequality. New Zealand is only one-quarter of 1 percent of the world’s
economy, so we are, in fact, negatively aff ected by what goes on in the rest of the
world. But if we continue to do things ri ght, as this John Key - led Government is
doing, it will, conversely, have a positive e ffect on New Zealand, like stimulating new
jobs and delivering those better services for families that we talk about, while staying on
track for surplus in 2014-15.
Budget 2012 sees this National Government  investing in welfare reforms—an
upfront investment of $287 million over the ne xt 4 years in the first phase of the
reforms. The second phase of the reform s will be funded by Budget 2013. Yes, it will
cost more up front to save over the long te rm. We have always said that. But this
translates to more support to help people o ff welfare and into work. The entire welfare
package is expected to cost at least $520 m illion and is expected to save $1 billion over
4 years, and, to me, that is good budgeting.
We will keep protecting vulnerable New Zealanders through Working for Families,
New Zealand superannuation, and welfare benefits. However, we believe that those who
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4349
can actually work should work. We have sa id that over and over again. People who can
work should work. That is why, as part of th e first phase of the we lfare reforms, we are
investing $287.5 million in education and training. These reforms are designed to
provide better support for beneficiaries, to help encourage them back to the workforce.
This Government cares about our young New Zealanders. Funding for youth services
will provide budgeting and parenting courses,  milestone payments to providers, and
wraparound support, as well as  financial assistance to you ng people. Youth providers
will work with unemployed or disengaged young people, and teen parents, too, to get
them into education, get their National Ce rtificate of Educational Achievement level 2,
or get into training. Even financial assistan ce for contraception is included in Budget
2012. We know that some on welfare find cost  is a barrier to accessing long-acting
reversible contraception, so we are removing that barrier.
Wider welfare changes include a new work-f ocused benefit called jobseeker support,
a part-time work expectation for sole parents with children over 5, a full-time work
expectation for sole parents with childre n aged over 14, a new sole parent support
benefit to replace the DPB, and a new suppor ted living payment to replace the invalids
benefit and the DPB care of sick and infirm bene fit. It is an investment approach to the
welfare system, and I think it is something th at the Minister is leading in this area
around the world.
National’s Social Security  (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill has
passed into law, and starts our investment a pproach to welfare in this country. We need
to get the best results, based on an indivi dual’s likelihood of falling into the welfare
trap. We cannot see more young people falling into this trap of being dependent on
welfare. Too many people have been on benefits for far too long. We know that young
people who come on to a benefit early stay  on a benefit longer, and we know how
destructive long-term welfare dependency can be. Getting them off welfare and into
work means a better life, bette r opportunities, and a brighter  future for them and their
dependants, their children, and their families. That is why we are overhauling and
modernising the welfare system. We started with Future Focus changes, which
introduced greater expectations , and the next step will be  the second phase of major
welfare reforms, which introduce new benef it categories and a greater focus on work.
This is a great Minister and a great Government, working hard for New Zealanders.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Primary Industries

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is a privilege to take a short
call on Vote Primary Industries and, in par ticular, to reflect the word from the
agricultural community, which is that National seems to have something against farmers
at the moment. The sad evidence of that fact  is in the cuts to front-line biosecurity
services—front-line services vital to protec ting our billion-dollar agricultural trade and
our export industry, which is worth thousands  and thousands of jobs. From these job
cuts, $2.8 million was saved, compared with th e billion-dollar cost of a foot-and-mouth
outbreak in New Zealand, or the 146 times greater cost of  the Psa outbreak in our
kiwifruit industry. The latest independent re port on the Psa disease shows that it will
cost our economy $410 million. That is 146 times the cost of the cuts to the staff.
John Key promised not to cut front-line services, but in 2009 his Government slashed
54 front-line biosecurity positions. More re dundancies have followed since, and the
latest figures show that there are now 91 fe wer biosecurity staff than previously. Even
Wellington Airport, in this fair city wher e we are standing, has not had a sniffer dog
working in it since October last year. That is gross negligence of duty by a Government
that is exposing our primary industries to undue risk. In fact, the number of detector
4350 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
dogs nationwide, I am advised, has dropped und er National, and last year only one new
dog—

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: Woof, woof!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: —was trained, compared with 15 in 2008. Members
opposite might snigger, but the reality is that  those dogs are our la st line of defence
when not every package can be opened on the biosecurity front.
Mr Carter, the Minister  for Primary Industries, said that  staff cuts were a result of a
drop in imports, but that just does not stack up, because, for example, since December
2009 the number of internati onal passengers arriving in Ne w Zealand has increased by
140,000 a year, and in December 2009 the value of imported cargo, including the cost
of insurance, increased by $6.9 million. So we  have more people, more imports, fewer
biosecurity staff, fewer detector dogs, and weaker protection. Maybe it is a coincidence
that we have had a tragic outbreak in our ki wifruit industry, but, frankly, that is not a
risk that New Zealanders should be taking.
I think this shows a broader point. This National Government is priding itself on
trying to balance the books, but it is fallin g into a very old, well-known problem. It
knows the cost of everything and the value of nothing. Penny-pinching a few bucks out
of biosecurity and prejudicing a billion-dollar industry is not smart.
The other word on the street is that this new Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries
conglomerate is being dumbed down—dumbed down. It has forestry people working on
agriculture, and fisheries peopl e working on forestry. The whole thing is a mess. It is
like the Ministry of Business, Innovation a nd Employment, the great white whale that
blended the Ministry of Economic Developm ent and the science ministries, which has
saved nothing, given Mr Joyce an empire, but contributed nothing back to industry.
The Government does not have a substant ive plan—not a real strategy—so it is
moving the deckchairs around amongst the Pub lic Service to give the impression of
movement. The thing is that farmers are pr etty smart people. They know the difference
between real work and make-work, and they  are not fooled by a bureaucratic shuffle.
What they want is answers, and they want protection for biosecurity, and that is why the
Labour Party is standing up and saying that we  disagree with those cuts to front-line
biosecurity services.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: The Labour Party hates you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: The Labour Party, Attorney-General, the Labour Party—
exactly. Agriculture is New Zealand’s mainst ay. It is our primar y export sector. We
depend upon the protein, fine food products, wines, and other products from our
primary sector that we export. The Labour Party is committed to partnering with this
industry to help it to grow, to get more people in work, to incr ease the value of our
exports, and to bring higher technology, better jobs, and higher incomes to this sector.
We are willing and able to listen to the indus try about what it needs, and to partner with
it towards a future that is going to be more prosperous and more sustainable. Thank you.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: If there was ever an
example of why a bursary should be given back to a university and an apology should
be sent with it for ever accepting it, the member who just resumed his seat, David
Cunliffe, is probably a good example. He is  a Harvard graduate, now returned from
overseas as the new agriculture spokesman for Labour, from the seat, I think, of New
Lynn in west Auckland—a wonderful combin ation. The last time the member spoke to
a farmer was probably before he went off overseas to further his education.
Why do we not look at some of the thi ngs that have happened? The member
mentioned that there have been no new det ector dogs trained. Well, I am pleased to
announce to the member that there are now fi ve new dogs that have just been trained
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4351
and made available in Welli ngton Airport alone, I understa nd, for the very purpose that
he spoke of.
But let us talk about some of the bigger issues: over half a billion dollars of
Government and industry investment in the Pr imary Growth Partnership. If we look at
how we can lift the standard of living in New Zealand, overwhelmingly it is going to be
by growing the areas that we are best at, which are our primary industries—our
agricultural exports, the exports from this country. So how do you innovate, how do you
develop products, and how do you meet mark et expectations? Well, by investing in
research and development. Developing the Primary Growth Partnership and investing
now close to half a billion dollars in that is, I guess, the single biggest contribution that
the State can make towards growing exports.
As for tackling greenhouse gas emissions, I do not think there is anybody in the
Chamber who suggests that we should not do ev erything we can as an export nation, as
an agricultural nation, to look at how we can make a sensible contribution—not the
Labour-type contribution of just taxing a nd hoping that something comes right, but a
sensible contribution. Putting $50 million into the Agricultural Greenhouse Gas
Research Centre is much more likely to return a dividend on that investment. Our
involvement in and the investments made in the Global Research Alliance on
Agricultural Greenhouse Gases mean that New Zealand is now being described all over
the world as a leader in this  field. Just imagine that: under Labour we were described as
dragging our feet, not having an  environmental policy, and not  looking in this area but
looking backwards; we are now seen as l eaders in the Global Re search Alliance on
Agricultural Greenhouse Gases. That is a very, very positive response from this
Government.
There will be $80 million in savings over 4 years from the combination of the
industries that the member just spoke of, and he suggested that  somehow this was
negative, and somehow this was dumbing down our primary sector. I would suggest to
you that just the opposite of what the member  suggested is happeni ng, and it is very
good to see that.
So what have we done here in Parliament in terms of the legislative programme that
is going to be useful and part of this great er growth in the primary sector? Well, the
passing of the Dairy Industry Restructuring Amendment Bill. There will be no greater
investment in New Zealand’s growth than  the work that was done to enhance the
country’s biggest export earner, which is our dairy industry—26 pe rcent of our exports
come from that sector. I note that someone  from the Green side of the Chamber or
someone over here chimed in on that. Let us just have a look at what our opponents are
talking about in regard to an alternative view of what  we should be doing. The first
thing they are talking about is a capital ga ins tax. I would like to know how that will
grow our export earnings and grow our primary sector. I have been in terested to listen
to the comments—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Haven’t you been listening?

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Well, I have been. I have not heard anything sensible: higher
income taxes, no support for irrigation, and an agricultural emissions tax. Well, you
know, how does that reduce greenhouse gase s—a drop in farm values through the
increase of taxes? I have heard about no more 90-day trials for new employees, and
rural New Zealand stuck in the dial-up age because Labour opposes the broadband roll-
out that this Government is involved in. Less road construction—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Oh, because there are so many roads being built in the regions!

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Well, look, I have listened to the arguments about how we
could have better development by enhancing public transport.
4352 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I will eventually take up the roads of
national significance, but, firs t of all, I want to congratul ate the Minister for Primary
Industries and his Associate Mi nister. In fact, I want to congratulate also the Primary
Production Committee, which drives this sector . We have listened tonight to the debate
on Vote Social Development and the investment that the Ministry of Social
Development needs to make in this countr y. Well, I can assure you the investment is
going to be driven by the Ministry for Primary Industries.
I want to touch briefly on the roads of nati onal significance. I also  want to touch on
the railways, because both of those are criti cal to the success of the primary production
sector in New Zealand. In f act, the roads of national si gnificance are how we get our
exports to the port. The fact that there are very few roads of national significance in Mr
Ardern’s electorate has got nothing to do with it, because in fact once he gets them on to
those roads of national significance, they get to the port much more efficiently.
I also want to talk briefly about the railways and the sign ificance of the railways to
New Zealand. For anyone who observes th e railways running through Palmerston
North, you will see that on a daily  basis there are a signifi cant number of milk trains,
fertiliser trains, and, indee d, other trains carting products, logs, and whatever else from
the agricultural sector of New Zealand to th e ports. So the railways too are critical to
our future.
I want to talk also about the investment the Government has made in science and
technology. I want to go back in history a litt le bit in doing so, because for a while the
agricultural sector has struggled to keep its share of i nvestment in the development of
science and technology—in fact, in the deve lopment of its future. It has become
extremely critical to agriculture that we continue to invest heavily in science. I want to
speak briefly about the Riddet Institute, whic h is a part of Massey University, and, of
course, based in my electorate. This inst itute is led by Professors Paul Moughan and
Harjinder Singh. They come up with all sort s of new strategies  and new innovative
ideas for boosting the production and use of our agricultural pr oducts. I think it is very
exciting. It is a very exciting institute, and it is the futu re of New Zealand’s export
industries. I think this type of  development is certainly the future of this type of new
product and new development that is going to  take place in the food and agricultural
production sectors.
A lot of attention has been paid over recent weeks to the declining rural population in
New Zealand. This Government takes this issu e very seriously. The demise of services
suffered in the first 10 years of the 2000s, and before that, around education, health, and
other factors—and, indeed, of investment in  our roading infrastru cture in those years—
has caused issues in rural New Zealand that  have certainly incited the lowering of
population in some of the towns and villages in rural New Zealand. It  is a problem that
we need to reverse the trend of, and th is Government will reverse that trend by
continuing strong investment in education, th e health sectors, and maintaining a strong
hand in our economy in times of significant difficulty around the world.
So I am very impressed with the investme nt this Government is putting into the
primary production sector. I am very impr essed with the leadership the primary
production sector has from this Government , and I think we are in very good hands.
Thank you.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Foreign Affairs and Trade

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: The Minister of Foreign Affairs has
signalled that he is going. He is going to  New York to be ambassador there, and,
believe, me, it cannot come too soon. This Mini ster was so keen to  appear before the
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4353
estimates committee that he turned up at 1 o’clock on the Thursday afternoon, 1 hour
before the House sat, on the very last day of  estimates! He could not have left it any
longer. We had given him 6 weeks in which to appear, and he chose the very last
minute—and no wonder. This Minister has to go because he has made an absolute botch
of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Tr ade and its reorganisation—and John Hayes is
wanting to nod there, but he cannot quite bring himself to do it because the boss might
be watching.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trad e that I remember was committed, it was
competent, it was absolutely efficient, it was professional, and he took that ministry and
turned it into a disillusioned and dispirit ed organisation in the space of 3 years. You
know, the ministry does a survey of how enga ged its employees are. And what did that
survey find? It found that 14 pe rcent, or one in nine, were  positive about their job at
foreign affairs—14 percent. Fifty-seven pe rcent were ambivalent—they did not know
whether they still wanted to work in that  organisation—and 28 pe rcent were negative.
This was a professional foreign service, one of  the best ministries in this country, and
one of the best small ministries in the wo rld, and that is Mr McCully’s legacy. And
why—why? It was all to save how much? Twelve million dollars.
Mr McCully destroyed a professional or ganisation to save $12 million. It is
absolutely unprecedented: 49 heads of mi ssion—we have about 53 of them—the most
able and experienced civil servants we have in  the foreign service, wrote a letter saying
that the steps Mr McCully had initiated w ould damage for years our ability to pursue
our economic and trade interests. That was th e conclusion of our t op civil servants in
foreign affairs. And what did he pay to do  this reorganisation? Well, he spent $10
million on consultants—$10 million on consultants—and seconded staff, and $6 million
in redundancy, all to produce a crock that he had to disavow halfway through the
process. He blames John Allen. Who is John Allen? John Allen is the chief executive
officer of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. He is a civil servant now. He
cannot answer back, and it is lacking in cour age for any Minister to treat their chief
executive officer like that.
But what did we find in the examination in  the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee? We found that long before Murray McCully owned up to knowing about it,
he knew that 300 people were on the line to  lose their jobs, he knew that 600 staff
would have to reapply for thei r jobs, he knew that the local staff in our agencies around
the world were going to be s acked, he knew that the allowan ces paid to civil servants
who took their family overseas to a posting we re going to be savaged, and he knew that
there was a plan to close down multiple European posts. That was the plan. Murray
McCully knew about it from the start. He bl amed John Allen, but the truth of the matter
is this: that plan would have gone ahead but for a full-scale rebellion on the part of our
most professional civil servants, and the a nger and dismay of the stakeholders who
knew that New Zealand’s interests in trad e and security intern ationally depended on
foreign affairs, who said “This has got to stop”, and they pulled the reins in on Murray
McCully.
I want to say that one other thing came out of the select committee, and it was the
cult of secrecy. This Minister, Murray Mc Cully, was a Minister who censored two-
thirds of the briefing to him as the incomi ng Minister of Foreign Affairs, and at the
select committee could not justify cutting that information out. This is the only Minister
in the House who has withheld, and who con tinues to withhold, Trea sury’s briefing on
the portfolio responsibility.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: One of the issues that we have in the
foreign affairs portfolio is, I thought, an understanding that party politics stop at the
border, and I feel deeply disappointed because  offshore we need to be there as “New
4354 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Zealand Inc.”, all working together for a common cause. So I take some exception to the
member Phil Goff’s attack on my colleague Murray McCully, who I think has done an
absolutely superb job in picking up the pieces  left by that last speaker and moving them
and New Zealand and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade on to a new plane.
Let me just set out some of the Minister of Foreign Affairs’ achievements. First, New
Zealand’s exports to China have increased by 150 percent between 2008 and 2012.
India and New Zealand signed several agreemen ts during the Prime Mi nister’s visit in
2011 in, for example, education and films. Progress has been made on the free-trade
agreement with Russia, because that ma rket has increased its food imports by 500
percent to 2000. Russia is one  of the world’s largest ma rkets for the importation of
butter and cheese, and New Zealand’s expo rts to Russia in 2011 were worth $120
million. New Zealand signed a new accord with our third-largest trading group,
ASEAN, that is already worth $4.6 billion to our export market. And after 90 years—
and a 10-year effort by Mr Goff that got us nowhere—we have got our apples back into
Australia. Yes, Murray McCully achieved that, not Phil Goff. Our Australian and New
Zealand CER investment protocol was signed by the Prime Minister on 16 February last
year, and we have got ongoing negotiations with Korea.
Under the Minister’s leadership there is always more to do. That is why he is so busy
travelling the world, because he is putting stu ff in place for us. We have to develop a
comprehensive programme of Government-led trade delegations to China, India, and
ASEAN. We have got 28 trade missions to be led by Minist ers over the next 3 years.
Our drive and focus on New Zealand agencies and interaction and the release of a series
of New Zealand country strategies goes on.
Let us come back and reflect on the comment s made by the last speaker. We are in a
situation where this country is in recession  and no stone is going to  be left unturned by
this Government to get our economy back into surplus by 2014. Part of that requires the
foreign affairs ministry—a directive from Cabinet—to save $24 million a year in each
of the next 3 years. That is why John Allen,  as chief manager of  the foreign affairs
ministry, made the interventions that he di d, and those interventions, despite the efforts
of that last speaker, are progressing well.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Yeah, right! What’s the attrition rate? How many have left? They’re
leaving in droves.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Well, I can promise you it was not the 300 that you just spoke
about. In fact—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Mr Chair, I can promise you that that speaker was absolutely wrong
to be asserting that 300 people are going to leave. That is  not the case, and was never
the original plan.
I want also to congratulate the foreign affairs Minister on the wonderful work that he
has done on Fiji, and on getti ng Fiji and the region engaged. I think back to 2000, when
the then Prime Minister, Helen Clark, and he r foreign affairs Minister, one Phil Goff,
were driven in their response by the commun ity of Fijian Indians who came into the
South Auckland electorates and drove them. Th ey said: “Let us put up barriers to that
Government. Let us refuse to speak to them .”, and we refused to speak to them for 9
years. For 9 long years that member refused to speak to the Fijians. Well, I am very
grateful for the leadership  shown personally by Murray McCully, who has worked his
backside off this year as leader of the fo rum group of foreign Mini sters who have been
engaged with Fiji, and they have made sign ificant progress. They have made significant
progress in getting Fiji back into the fl ock, and that Minist er, Mr McCully, has
committed significant money to enable the re gistration of Fijians in the electoral
process. I have no doubt that an election will take place in 2014.
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4355

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: In our Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee’s report we noted that the new a ppropriations show a 20 percent increase
over the previous year. One might think half a billion dollars is not excessive for foreign
affairs and trade for a country that is hi gh on the GDP and the United Nations Human
Development Index rankings. Of course, ou r overseas development assistance is down,
showing the world how miserly we can be ev en in times of aust erity. Tough times are
when the poor around the world are in the grea test need. Our response is to pull up the
drawbridge, export more food to increase in come, evince an illusory complacency in
our ecological surplus, and cut our aid. Congr atulations to the Minister of Foreign
Affairs on being his existential self.
The ministry is described as undergoing “t he most profound structural, cultural, and
technological reform …” in its history. Th at is one way of putting it. Whatever the
change, it is not for the better. Transmogrif ication for “New Zealand Inc.” would be
more apt—change with an ideological warp with no stone left unturned, with special
ministerial eccentricity thrown in. The aim, we were told, was for the ministry to
become more flexible, more focused, and less expensive. The outcome, we can assume,
risks being more craven, more neurotic, and le ss worthy. It appears to be lost on this
trader Government that governance is a matter of values. It is a matter of values, and
values come with a price. Yet values, not least in foreign policy, are what count, and the
challenge is to ensure that the price is worthwhile. The price tag appears to be all that
this Minister values, which makes for a nice, ironic, circular logic.
And values have something in turn to do w ith our international reputation, which has
something to do with our bid for the United Nations Security Council seat. This is likely
to come back to haunt us in coming years.  In assessing whether a UN member State is
ready for service on the council, other count ries tend to scrutinise your record. We
believe we are among the most enlightened of  UN member States. This is because we
focus selectively on what we believe we are good at. Others have the temerity to look at
the total picture. So curbing our overseas development assistance percentage from an
already low ranking will cost against us. So will cutting our contribution to the UN
demining project. So will withdrawing from  United Nations Industrial Development
Organisation, whose mission is to assist th e 5 billion poor switch to a green economy.
So will failing to do our fair share in carbon mitigation. So will telling the Rio+20 Earth
Summit in June that the switch to a green economy requires a pragmatic approach, not a
new paradigm. And, above all, so will insist ing on wriggle room for the use of one’s
armed forces.
In a major public speech recently the Minister sternly warned an unsuspecting world
that New Zealand would not lay down c onditions for its candidacy. We would not
attempt to buy a seat on the council either  by spending taxpayer dollars or by changing
policy. He need have no fear . Recording 0.26 percent of our official development
assistance runs no risk whatsoever of the world suspecting we are buying our way on to
the council. It would be more inclined to suspect that of our main rival—Spain spends
0.43 percent. We spend half a billion dollars; Spain spends $6 billion. And there is to be
no change of policy. That, of course, begs the question of what the policy is. During that
address extolling our candidacy, the Minister refused to confine future national military
action to Security Council auth orisation. What an extraordin ary situation! In advancing
a candidacy for United Nations Security C ouncil membership, New Zealand will not be
bound in its military operations by the United Nations Charter, which it has signed up
to. Let there be no misunderstanding here . The Green Party endorses a New Zealand
seat on the council, but this Government fails the required test—that of being a
responsible global citizen.
4356 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Recently I proposed to the Foreign Affair s, Defence and Trade Committee that it
undertake a study on UN reform. It is not too la te to adopt a cross- party dialogue about
how we might work together, iron out a few differences, and e nhance our candidacy
together.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Official Development Assistance agreed to.
Vote Sport and Recreation agreed to.
Vote Corrections agreed to.
Vote Police

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on this
particular aspect of this estimates debate , being a former police officer. Can I firstly
start off by commending the work of the New Zealand Police, led by a very constructive
and front line - focused commander in Peter Marshall. It is my view that the New
Zealand Police, indeed, set the standar d—set the bar—for policing globally. This
country can feel very well served by the men and women of the New Zealand Police,
out there on a daily basis, often putting thei r lives on the line to make our communities
a safer place. I just want to acknowle dge the men and women of the New Zealand
Police in that regard.
It is fair to say that 2011 has been a nother successful year for the New Zealand
Police, with a 4.8 percent reduction in recorded crime. We now have recorded crime at a
15-year low. I can certainly recall as a police officer that  I sometimes did wonder what
sort of smoke and mirrors made up some of the statistics, but I think it is very fair to say
that what we are really looking for is a trend. The trend has been a consistent downward
trending in recorded crime. That means there are fewer victims, there is less harm in our
communities, there is less cost to our co mmunities, and, most important, we can go
about our business in our communities feeling sa fer. That in some part will be a result
of the some 600 more front-line police th at the New Zealand public can now feel
assured in having in their service, but also I believe much of the credit must go to the
Prevention First approach, which has been ad opted since this Nati onal-led Government
came into office.
Indeed, some very positive changes have been made in the executive of the New
Zealand Police, and it has embraced the noti on that preventing the problem is going to
be a lot easier than coming al ong afterwards and trying to a rrest your way out of it. I
want to speak to that to some extent, an d I will come back to that, but certainly
addressing drivers of crime is fundamental in reducing overall crime.
The investment that has been made by th e New Zealand Police and this Government
is certainly showing the ri ght trending, reflecting this approach. Of course, this
approach runs hand in hand with the reform s right across the ju stice and corrections
sector. It is fair to say that the police them selves do not stand alone in ensuring that our
communities are safer places. For example, in justice—if I can just reflect for a
moment—we have brought in maximum jail sentences with no parole for the worst
offenders. There are tougher sentences for pe ople who commit crimes against children,
which is something I know that right across this House we all share a great deal of
concern about, and it is fair to say that we are all committed to making a difference to
those innocent young child victims.
Introducing stronger bail laws is part of the programme in this space, as is reversing
the burden of proof for some of the most se rious offences. As a former serving police
officer, I can honestly say that that will pr ovide a position where those who often walk
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4357
free from a court and go on to commit offences while on bail will be denied that
opportunity. We do not have to  look too far to see the very  tragic examples of where
that has happened. So I am very pleased to see that particular bill moving forward. Of
course, reducing the situ ations where defendants are bailab le as of right does actually
encapsulate a number of offences and offe nders. When people commit crimes against
society, I think it is fair to say that the onus, first and foremost, should actually be on the
law-abiding citizens—their safety and protections. So I think there will be some positive
changes there also.
Of course, the police and justice sector also serves in the process of safer
communities with the service within corrections. It is another area where there has been
a significant investment by this Government in turning round what has been, to some
extent, a holding pen for some of this country ’s worst offenders, who ultimately will be
released into society. Our goal must be, surely, to ensure that they are not going back
into the justice system, so a lot of effort  has been put into having more prisoner
education and employment programmes. Dr ug and alcohol treatment has increased
significantly and it will continue to do so. When you consider that  certainly around
some 85 to 90 percent of offenders will enter the justice and corrections system with a
drug and/or alcohol problem, this is an investment in preventing reoffending. Of course,
there are more search powers for our correc tions officers, and we have fewer positive
drug tests and fewer prisoner escapes.
What we are really talking about here is  a pipeline and a set of agencies and
professionals serving New Zealanders, in trinsically linked and ensuring that our
communities are safer. This Government is prou d to say that we have put victims at the
heart of the justice system, and the New Z ealand Police certainly is mindful of the
prevention work in reducing the number of  victims. Ultimately, the best crime
prevention that can happen is, really, when it is focused on having fewer victims.
The $50 levy that this Gove rnment introduced has now serviced some 13 new
services for victims, which is an interesti ng concept. That money is being put to very
good use.
Victims now have a greater ability to have  their say by way of their victim impact
statements. I can again reflect on times when victims of crime had their one opportunity
to stand up, to face their offender, and to expr ess their real feelings about how they had
been wronged as they went about their lives innocently. The ability for them to do that
in an open and unencumbered manner is ofte n the difference between them being able
to move on or not, so I applaud that.
Of course, the police now have extra powers to enforce on-the-spot protection orders.
Some 6,000 of those safety orders have been issued since their inception, which
ultimately means there are fewer victims.
Our police are really at the sh arp end of this pipeline th at I have been describing.
Their Prevention First approach is really fundamentally what I think has been the game-
changer and has led to some of these very  impressive statistics in terms of the
downward trending. Of course, one victim is one too many, but we have to be realistic
in that regard. The success, I believe, is a legacy of both Minister  Collins and Minister
Tolley, who has picked up from the very good work being done there.
I would have to say that Prevention First has not always been the case. I remember
back as a police officer who joined in the mid-1990s. With the Doone era—and some
interesting dilemmas there—and the introducti on of the Clark Government, the police
very much moved to a commercial model, where we were driven by statistics. Theft and
burglary were on a significant increase, and, quite rightly, pol ice were aimed at
targeting that. Of course, a big part of the reason for that was the burgeoning
methamphetamine problem, which went from virtually nothing to the worst in the world
4358 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
between 1998 and 2003. When you have got  a $1,000-a-day methamphetamine habit,
you are going to commit a lot of volume crime.
I believe that the leadership of the Prime Mi nister in this space with regard to the
methamphetamine strategy and the way in  which the New Zealand Police have
