embraced Prevention First are all very good arguments as to why New Zealand is a
safer place today. With our hard-working Mini sters, an excellent executive within the
police, and dedicated serving police officers, I think we sh ould all be proud of our men
in blue. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am both happy and disillusioned to be making
this call on the Appropriation (2012/13 Estimates ) Bill on behalf of New Zealand First.
I am disillusioned—more than a little disillusioned—when I look at the Vote Police
allocation, and, more to the point, the fact  that, in real terms, it has not only not
increased but has actually gone backwards.
The police are the front line in the fight agai nst crime. They are the first point of call
for the public whenever danger threatens. They are the fabled thin blue line that stands
between the law-abiding citizen and the ev ildoer—it is a somewhat clichéd term
nowadays, but a valid one nonetheless. We are not giving them enough money. New
Zealand is not resourcing its police force well enough to enable them to do their jobs
properly—the job of protecting all of us and of preventing and solving crime. They do a
sterling job of their allotted task. That much is beyond question. Despite the lack of
proper recognition and the lack of sufficient funding and res ource allocation that this
Government affords them, the police keep  on keeping on. They keep on keeping the
villain at bay, and they keep on putting themselves on the line, and putting life and limb
in the way of danger, so the rest of us ma y enjoy a measure of relative safety. As the
quote from George Orwell says: “We sleep sa fe in our beds because rough men stand
ready in the night to visit violence on those who would do us harm.”
The police men and women of New Zealan d, the rough and the not so rough,
undeniably stand amongst that good number, al ong with the men and the women of our
equally beleaguered and under-resourced defe nce forces. Despite this reality, we deny
them the money they need in order to prot ect us. We skimp on the important things in
this country. Too often we a llocate resources in a manner th at stands the priorities of
logic on their head. The police need more money, not less. This vote, this appropriation,
this Budget has failed them. It fails us; it fails the people of New Zealand. The police
are the ones who are called on to come out at night to de al with the drunks and the
reprobates, to be shot at and spat at, and threatened and stabbed with knives and
screwdrivers and syringes fill ed with God knows what. They clean up after bar brawls
and street fights and car crashes. They te ll grieving parents and family members that
their children and thei r loved ones are not coming home, a nd in return we give them a
flat budget, a negative budget,  and what is in reality a backwards budget. We should be
paying them more, but in reality we are paying them less.
There will be no pay round for New Zealand’s police men and women this year.
They will have to do ever more with ever less, as this Government requires the police to
find cuts and savings from what is alr eady an insufficient allocation. Knives and
screwdrivers and dirty syringes, I say to the members opposite, some of whom have had
real life experience in the blue uniform—an d I salute them for that. I salute my
colleagues opposite who have served in the bl ue uniform, who have been part of that
thin blue line. Knives and screwdrivers a nd dirty syringes, and no chance of a pay rise
for the next year, thank you very much. We are told we are in—o r at least we have
been—the middle of a recession, a global financial meltdown, a crisis of some kind or
another. Because of this, everyone has to ti ghten their belts. Well, that comes back to
priorities again, and I wonder if perhaps the Government could have held off buying
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4359
new limousines for a year or so longer and given the police a pay rise instead. I wonder
about things like that.
We are told that crime is reducing. Really ? There is less reported crime? Hurrah. Or
is there—is there really? Is there actually less crime, or is the drop in some forms of
reported crime really just a drop in reporti ng? In the year ending 31 December between
2010 and 2011, reported sex crimes, sexual assa ult and related offences increased. So
did unlawful entry with intent, burglary, and breaking and entering. Also on the increase
were miscellaneous offences, whatever they  may encompass. At the same time, fewer
than half of all reported crimes over the same period were actually solved. The total
resolution rate for the year ended 31 December 2011 was 47 percent. Maybe people just
simply are not bothering to report crim e because they know that our hopelessly
underfunded police force does not have the ti me or manpower to do anything about it.
Resolution of sexual offences was just 56 perc ent, resolution of robbery and extortion
cases was 43 percent, and resolution of cases involving unlawful  entry, burglary, and
breaking and entering was just 15 percent—one in six. Theft cases solved came in at 23
percent, and property damage was 30 percent.
Against this backdrop, we are telling the police they cannot have any more money,
they cannot have a pay rise, and they are not  getting any more tool s and resources with
which to do their job. In fact , we are telling them they ar e going to have to have more
paperwork to do because we are cutting back -office staff positions as well. Front-line
cops will have more administrative tasks to do, so that will take them away from their
front-line duties.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on Vote
Police, and I would just like to also ac knowledge and congratul ate Minister Tolley,
Police Commissioner Marshall, Deputy Polic e Commissioner Mike Bush, and Deputy
Police Commissioner Viv Rickard. In a servi ce like the police, strong leadership does
matter. You will get results and good morale  through strong leadership, and the police
service at the moment is enjoying very strong leadership.
I would like to talk a little bit about the two pillars that the police commissioner has
announced and that Minister Tolley has a nnounced as being the cornerstone of how
policing is going to be rolled out and conti nue to move forward. For me it is quite an
exciting change and it is really a fundament al change in the way the police are doing
business and the way that they are serving our  communities. It is actually a change not
just within the police service. We have the Minister for Social Development here today
as well, and I have to say that her ministry is taking the same approach. Historically, the
police or Government agencies were often s een as fairly threatening or intimidating
organisations to engage with, for people to go in and seek help from, and I think that
with the first pillar, which is Prevention Fi rst, the police are going a long way towards
actually breaking down those barriers, getting rid of those historical barriers, and getting
out into the community more.
Going back to when I served, a lot of what we did, really, was reactionary. We would
get in our police vehicles at the beginning of  a shift and we would go out and we would
react. We would attend to jobs , and we would not really interact with the community a
lot outside of that initial response. Our co mmunity constables were tasked with doing
that and they were just a very, very small number.
We have had what are called the nei ghbourhood policing teams, which are now
being deployed around the country, and I would just like to take the opportunity to
commend the area commander in my own elect orate, Inspector Scott Webb, and his
team, because we have actually been very successful. They have rolled out the
Prevention First model in the electorate. It is working very well and it is getting
fantastic feedback from the community.
4360 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
But in the last 2 or 3 months I have been  able to get out a nd visit the Warkworth
Police Station, the Whangapar āoa Police Station, Ōrewa, Tauranga with Minister
Bridges yesterday, and Coun ties-Manukau. We were lucky as the Law and Order
Committee to actually go up to Counties-Manuk au and have a look and see what they
are doing with their neighbourhood policing teams.  I have to say that it is very, very
impressive how they are rolling that programme out and how they are really getting into
the communities now. Not only were the police officers on these neighbourhood
policing teams extremely enthusiastic about it —and it is a major shift in the way that
they think and the way that they do business,  and you could see that they had taken real
ownership of the communities and the areas th at they were responsible for—but it is
obvious that the communities are responding to it as well. And when you see these guys
out there, every day they will go out and they will put community meetings together.
They have got a marquee that th ey will just take out to a local  park. They will put it up,
and they will get everyone out of their house s and out into the park. They will actually
interact with them, find out what the real issues are in the communities, and then start to
be proactive in how they addr ess them. This is a really big, fundament al change in the
way that policing is being done in New Zealand. I think that it is going to go from
strength to strength, and we will continue to see the great results that we are seeing.
Coming back to social development, this is the same model that is being rolled out as
well, in many ways—these barriers are be ing broken down, and all of a sudden people
are feeling confident interac ting with Government departme nts, which before they may
not have felt very comfortable about.
In relation to policing and seeing a higher presence of police out on the streets, I
remember in 2005 I drove from Auckland down to Taup ō, a trip that I made fairly
regularly. Because I policed in that area, I always took an interest  in seeing how many
police were actually out on the road. In 2005 I made a trip from Auckland to Taup ō and
did not see one police car or one patrol in that  whole time on State Highway 1. This
year I made the same trip and I saw nine patrols between Auckland and Taupō.
When I visit these police stations, and in particular Tauranga yesterday, the thing that
strikes me is that you will walk into a mess room, into an area where normally the guys
are working, and there will be only two or three policemen in there. The rest of them are
out on the street—the rest of them are out in  the community. I think that this is a very,
very positive thing for our communities. Th ey are seeing their police out there more.
They are taking more of a Prevention First ap proach, where they are actually getting in
there and identifying what the issues are befo re they even become issues, rather than
reacting. So I just think that this is a very good model, and I know we are going to
continue to see fantastic results. Thank you.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Serious Fraud agreed to.
Vote Defence

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I begin my contribution
this evening by acknowledging the service and sacrifice of Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer
and Lance Corporal Rory Malone, and also acknowledging their families, who have lost
a son, a brother, a nephew, and a partner, a nd who have given up their loved ones in the
service of this nation. I think we should all be  mindful of that as we carry through this
debate this evening.
The Government promised New Zealand that the Defence Force under National
would be able to do more with less. But al l that the Minister of Defence, Jonathan
Coleman, has achieved is to drive down the morale within our armed forces to the
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4361
lowest level it has ever been. There are more  of our Defence Force personnel lining up
to leave today than there have ever been before. Engagement is trending downwards day
after day, and it is not just getting worse; it is getting worse at a faster rate now that it
has at any point before. So whilst this G overnment has presided over 2 years of
mismanagement of the defence forces, they have not even been able to tidy up their act;
it is getting worse now than it has ever been getting before.
There are a number of reasons  for this, but there are two that we can probably point
to. One reason is the terribly mismanaged process of civilianisation, which this
Government foisted upon the defence forces, and which they now accept was an
absolute failure. In fact, the second round of civilianisation will not go ahead, because it
has had such a detrimental impact on our defence forces. The second reason for such
poor morale in our defence forces is the 4- year wage freeze that has occurred under this
National Government. It is no wonder that pers onnel are lining up to leave. In fact, they
are leaving at such a rate that there ar e 1,000 fewer personnel in the defence forces
today than there were 2 years ago. That is  not intentional. The Government did not
intend for there to be 1,000 fewer personnel in  the defence forces than there were 2
years ago. This is a direct reflection of the absolute mismanagement of our defence
forces by this Government. Skilled personne l are walking away from our Defence
Force, because the Minister, Jonathan Colema n, has made such a hash of his job. Those
people are walking away, and, although we  have new people coming on board, the
defence forces are losing those skills.
It has got so bad that the attr ition rate in the navy is 22.3 percent. Because of that we
cannot put our inshore patrol vessels to sea. How ridicul ous is it that we have new
equipment tied up at Devonport, unable to be put to sea, because we do not have the
crew to get them out doing their job patr olling our exclusive economic zone? Members
of the SAS are lining up to  leave—our most important ground forces, our most
specialised ground forces. We are losing thos e skills as well. And I tell you what, those
personnel are deeply unhappy with our Minister , because he said: “Look, they have just
got to get over it.” He said: “But you’ve got  to remember, you’ve got guys in there who
have been there 25 or 30 years. They’ve been used to a job-for-life culture. The reality
is the NZDF has to come in line with the rest of the world.” It was that line—that the
New Zealand Defence Force has a job-for-l ife culture—that went down like a cup of
cold sick amongst Defence Force personnel, a nd they have reacted against our Minister
by lining up to leave.
It is not a job for life. It is  a calling. It is service. In the name of our nation we send
our men and women overseas, sometimes to die serving our nati on, and the Minister
had the gall to call it a job-for-life attitude. One member of the Defence Force has put it
to me like this. He said: “Look. We have no employment protec tions. We don’t fall
under the Employment Relations Act. We’ve got no bargaining. We’ve got no unions.
We serve our nation, and we  expect our nation to reciprocate that service, to
acknowledge that service.”

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Thank you very much for the opportunity
to speak in this part of the debate on the Appropriation (2012/13 Estimates) Bill, and on
the New Zealand Defence Force. I would like to begin by adding my condolences to the
families of the two soldiers who lost their lives in Afghanistan, and extending to the six
wounded soldiers best wishes from this House for a very speedy recovery. Their
sacrifice outlines why our Defence Force is so vital: to help protect New Zealand people
and territory, to conduct and lead missions with key allies , particularly in the South
Pacific, and to enable New Zealand to become a stronger partner in regional and
international security.
4362 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
I want to commend the Mini ster of Defence, Jonathan Coleman, because he has
given the Defence Force a direction and a l ong-term strategy—something it desperately
needed after 9 years without any Government  leadership. The Government’s vision is
for a joint amphibious task force, capable of sustained independent deployment, and
also capable of functioning as a credible part of a wider coalition. All capability
decisions are being made with this vision  in mind. Decisions ar e being made with
regard to how one capability, or a piece of equipment, works with another, and how this
fits within the vision for defence. In short, National has a plan for defence, and it is led
by our Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Yeah, run it down, into the ground.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: In contrast, the man interjecting across the House cut valuable
equipment from the service without any plan on  how to sell it, a nd he gave 210 people
the sack, as Labour cut them. Labour bought ex pensive equipment without any plan on
how to move or deploy it, a nd also showed so little respect for defence that it made
Mark Burton the Minister. I will not forg et, in 2005, when I firs t stood for Parliament,
the announcement by Mr Goff and Helen Clark a week before the election that they had
sold the Skyhawks for an amount of $155 million.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: No, you’ve got that absolutely wrong.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Yes, they did that the week be fore the election in 2005, and I got
straight on the phone to Don Brash and said “Don, these guys are te lling porkies.” That
$155 million sale turned into a $37 million cost because they were unsold, and 210
people lost their jobs on the back of that incompetence, Mr Goff.
These are tight financial times, and we ha ve maintained Defence Force spending and
we are looking to redistribute savings to fund the changes needed to make a 21 st
century, effective Defence Force. The New Zealand Defence Force has achieved $143
million of annual reoccurring efficiencies in  the last 12 months. These have been
reinvested in military capability. The Ne w Zealand Defence Force will deliver $350
million to $400 million of efficiencies back into the Defence Force by 2014-15. The
New Zealand Defence Force has saved $9.7 million through tougher negotiations with
contractors and consultants, a further $12.2 million through consolidation of some
training functions, such as driver traini ng, and it has saved another $7.9 million from
efficiencies in health services. The Government went looking  for efficiencies and it has
found them, because we do not want to wa ste taxpayer money. We actually have to
look—those of us who are electorate MPs—in to constituents’ ey es and say “We’re
doing the job well, and we’re spending your money sensibly and wisely.”
As a result of those savings, we are br inging in new capabilities. We will be
replacing the medium and heavy vehicle fleet,  to ensure that we can take our trucks
overseas, and drivers will be protected from improvised explosive devices. That is an
improvement that Labour never got around to doing. We are bringing in a littoral
warfare support group. Two new vessels are cu rrently being built in Northland. These
are vessels that can be deployed from a ship or a Hercules, to protect our larger vehicles,
anywhere in the world.
But whenever a saving is identified, it is condemned by the Opposition. The $18.6
million in annual recurring savings in civili anisation has been condemned, the $9.3
million in recurring savings from the Rese rve Force reform has been condemned, and
even the $630,000 in annual savings from the band reduction was condemned. So would
the Opposition have borrowed that extra $142 million per annum? Would it increase
that to $350 million or $400 million per annum, or would it cut capability? Would it not
replace the trucks? Would it not have a litto ral warfare support force, and not replace
the Seasprites? Would it not have upgraded the artillery?
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4363
The Opposition has identified one saving in this House. Mr Goff wants to cut the
defensive weapon upgrade for the frigates—a on e-off capital saving that he has called
“skyrockets for the boys”. This is a cut that  would mean deploying vessels to some of
the most hostile environments in the world, without the ability to defend themselves
from anti-shipping missiles. That is what  the Defence Force and the New Zealand
public know is the Labour Party approach to defence—borrow and spend. Do not look
at savings or long-term viability, and instead pin the tail on the donkey with cutting
capability. That is an Opposition that puts bands over military capab ilities. This is a
Government that recognises the need for re form, develops a pla n, and leads to it. I
congratulate the Minister on his excellence in this regard. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I would like, in sadness, to acknowledge
today the loss of Lance Corporal Pralli Du rrer and Lance Corporal Rory Malone—two
young men aged 26 who died s upporting their mates in ba ttle and whose lives were
sacrificed on behalf of th eir country. I want to pass on my personal sympathy—and, I
think, that of the House as a whole—to their families at their sad loss.
I have got to say that Mr Hayes did no credit to himself in the speech that he has just
delivered. He talked about cuts. I want to ta lk about cuts. I want to talk about the $25
million that they took out of the Budget last year that was designed to give our Defence
Force personnel their first wage rise in 4 years. Not content with cutting out $25 million
last year, they have cut out another $25 million this year. These are people who put their
lives at risk and who lose their lives, and the least we could do is respect them by giving
them a reasonable wage, taking into account 4 years of infla tion. All this Government
has done is cut the wages of those people who are serving their country.
You know you have got a weak Minister of Defence, a Minister lacking in
confidence, when you get a Minister who co mes to the Foreign Affairs, Defence and
Trade Committee and tries to filibuster hi s way through. You know, he had a 22-page
presentation—a 22-page presen tation—and after half an hour we said to the chairman:
“This has got to stop.” A select committee is about asking questions of the Minister, and
the Minister being accountable.
I will tell you why that Minister did not want to answer questions. It is set out here in
the presentation, on the very last page. It is called the Ongoing Attitude Survey. Do you
know what that shows? It shows that 40 pe rcent of our New Zealand Defence Force are
planning to leave—40 percent of  the Defence Force are planning to leave. What else
does it show? It shows that morale is at th e lowest level ever under this Government
since records began. It has dropped from 58 percent to 35 percent. That shows the
lowest level of morale that the Defence Force has ever had.
Mr Hayes talks about building up capability. I will tell you the capability he built up.
The Minister was forced to admit to the select committee that in just 2 years he had
slashed the Defence Force by 1,000 pers onnel—1,000 personnel. Were they spending
their money wisely? No, there was $9.5 million in redundancy, compared with
$250,000 in the last year of the Labour Government.
Who are the people that we are losing?  I asked the people down at the Devonport
naval base, and they said it is the chief petty officers. It is the petty officers, it is the
warrant officers, the people with trade sk ills, the people whom we have invested
hundreds of thousands of dollars in training, in  giving them those skills. They have 7 or
8 years’ experience and are in the prime of their career, and they are walking away
because they know there is a Government that does not care, that is not prepared to pay
them a decent wage, and that will not show th em respect. I say that that simply is not
good enough—the lowest level of engagement, the highest level of attrition.
Even in the SAS, a group I know well and have worked with on many occasions, 15
percent of the SAS badged members have left  in the last year—15 percent. The best
4364 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
trained, the most skilled, the elite unit of the New Zealand Army, and the members are
drifting away because of the policies of this Government.
That really is not good enough. You cannot leave people without a pay rise. You
cannot leave people without what they need  to carry out their job properly. That
Minister turned up at the select committ ee and said: “Look at what we’ve done—the
C130 programme, the programme for the Orion upgrade.” When did they start? It was
under a Labour Government. He talked  about the NH90 helicopters and the
AgustaWestland 108. Who ordered those and paid for them? It was a Labour
Government. This Government has done nothi ng but run down our Defence Force. It is
not good enough to slash the numbers by 1,000. It is not good enough to not pay them
enough. It is not good enough to cut their equipm ent, when these peop le are out there,
serving their country, dying for their country.  Surely they deserv e more respect than
that.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Defence Force agreed to.
Vote State Services agreed to.
Vote Energy

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased to stand and
speak in this estimates debate regarding energy and resources. The Government has set
ambitious economic goals for New Zealand, and that requires a significant improvement
in our economic performance. Productivity improvements are incremental as we gain
efficiency, but the highest area of productivity gain that we see in this country happens
through oil and gas exploration. Oil and gas production brings to this country a return of
$525,000 a year per fulltime-equivalent worker. Th at is a significant lift. In fact, when
you look at the top four export earners in this country—dairying, meat, timber, and oil
and gas—we note that when the T ūī Area field, which is just  offshore from Taranaki,
came into production, that one field lifted the industry to third place. So we see the
significance that just one significant oil disc overy can bring to the economic return to
this country.
Regarding the economic development of th is country, we have put together a
business growth plan that will grow more and bigger businesses in New Zealand and
provide the standard of living New Zealande rs aspire to. This business growth plan
touches on six key areas: capital markets; innovation a nd ideas; skilled and safe
workplaces; infrastructure, which includes elec tricity, broadband, and transport; export
markets; and the utilisation of natural reso urces. Obviously, the oil and gas sector relies
heavily upon all six of these. Oil is our fourth-largest expo rt earner, with a value of
around $2.2 billion a year. It contributes to the employme nt of approximately 7,700
within our country, 3,730 of which are direct jobs from that sector, and another 3,900 of
which are jobs in other parts of the ec onomy. We know that gas is an important
contributor to domestic industries and electr icity generation. We f ound this out so very
clearly last year when the M āui Gas pipeline north of New Plymouth was out of
commission for a week, with the effect that had on the economy of New Zealand,
particularly in the north. We also know that gas generated 18 percent of New Zealand’s
electricity supply in 2008.
All of that is to say that energy is a ve ry important area in our economy and in the
way of life for ordinary Ne w Zealanders. Energy underpins economic growth. Global
energy demand is forecast to increase by 40 percent between 2009 and 2035. So this is a
very important area. It is also very important  to understand that in order for this growth
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4365
to happen, it has to happen in a manner th at is well managed and consistent with the
wider values and the environmental values  we hold as a nation. The Government is
supporting the development of the oil and gas sector, which is set out in our petroleum
action plan. The aim of the plan is to ma ke the most of New Zealand’s promising
potential and maximise the gains from sector  growth in the petroleum area. Work is
well under way to streamline the management of the petroleum sector and to make it
easier for exploration companie s to establish operations in  New Zealand, whilst all the
time having stringent cautionary behaviours and activities around su ch exploration and
production.
We are currently reviewing the Crown Minerals Act regime. The Act governs
management of the Crown’s minerals estate, which includes all oil and gas. The review
aims to encourage development of our resources so they contribute to economic growth.
We aim to streamline the current regime and make it better able to deal with future
developments. We are reviewing health and safety regulations for petroleum operations,
and are advancing new environmental legi slation governing our exclusive economic
zone beyond the 12 nautical mile limit from ou r coast. All of these measures are put in
place in order for us to maximise the advantages and the gains, but by the same measure
to fulfil the obligations that these opportunitie s give us. From this year the Government
will be seeking a work programme for bids for 20 to 30 blocks annually. This is an
important step forward in the way New Z ealand is going to strategically manage
exploration interests. The bl ock offer strategically involve s exclusively using an annual
competitive tender process to allocate permits  for oil and gas exploration, and will no
longer use “first in, first served” permitting, known as priority in time. This allows
strategic management of the resource, focusi ng on areas of greatest potential, and this,
of course, ensures that we have the very be st of international practice regarding this
particular area of development in our economy.
I am very happy to speak in support of our energy and resources programme, which
we have put forward as a Government, and believ e that this is in the best interest of the
economic growth and development of our nation  as we, alongside that, ensure that we
have stringent and very careful environmen tal practices to suppor t those opportunities.
Thank you.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. It is good to take a call on the estimat es debate when it comes to energy. When you
follow that contribution from the member  Jonathan Young, you see everything this
Government is doing to support the industry. In this sector, the Government is quite
happy to pick winners. It is quite happy to th row taxpayers’ money at  specific sectors.
But what I want to look at in my speech is the economics. I think it  is foolhardy, it is
short-sighted, and it is not even in our economic  interest for us to be picking winners in
this sector when there are so many other better sectors we could be doing it for.
We heard today from the Minister of En ergy and Resources and his sort of seal
impersonation. Maybe more in my son’s co mprehension he sounded like the count off
Sesame Street, with his “Ah, ah, ah!”—the ghost of Muldoon. The Minister cannot even
count, because the numbers when it comes to the economics of oil just do not stack up.
This Government is putting offshore oil companies first, and the New Zealand
environment and the New Zealand taxpa yer second. But disappointingly for the
Government, its whole strategy is in tatter s at the moment. We have had the Anadarko
Petroleum Corporation pull out of the Sout h Island, and we have got New Zealand Oil
and Gas pulling out. The Government’s strategy is  in tatters. It has got no plan. It came
to the country with the Budget and said: “Our  plan is we’re going to drill it, mine it,
frack it, cut it, and sell it.” It is tryi ng to do the cut it and sell it plan, but New
4366 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Zealanders are standing up, lik e they are on the assets, and saying that there are better
options and that to drill it, mine it, and frack it is not the only option.
When you look at the economics, it does no t stack up. The Government is talking
about wanting to grow the export industry. In the best year we are talking about just
over $2 billion worth of exports . It is good to be earning fo reign currency, but what the
Government does not point out is  that oil is still one of our  biggest, if not the biggest,
imports. It is 16 percent of our imports—$8 bi llion. So if we are going to become an
exporter of oil, like the Minister’s briefing points out, we have got to massively increase
our production of oil. The only way we are going to do that is by drilling deep, very
deep down, and that comes with huge risks. We saw in the Gulf of Mexico that the
blowout there has cost $40 billion to date. It is in the exploratory stage, which we may
see Petrobras doing off the coast of the East Coast, which is the most dangerous phase.
It is not about just having a poke around; you are having a poke around in an
environment where you do not know the conditions. You do not know whether there are
gas bubbles. You do not know all the threats. That is its riskiest point.
What we know is that the Government is quite prepared to risk our environment; our
“clean, green” brand, which is worth over $20 b illion; our aquacultur e; our fisheries;
and our tourism industry. We know that Kiwis are going to be facing 100 percent of the
environmental risks, but when you look at th e income side of the ledger sheet, it does
not stack up. The Minister himself concedes that we have got the fourth-lowest royalty
plus tax rate in the world, se lling ourselves as cheap as almo st any other country on the
planet. We know that the Government has made a sweetheart deal for the oil industry. It
has put a dozen jobs on the ski lls shortages immigration list, so we know that what jobs
there will be will go to foreigners. We know th at Taranaki, which the Minister likes to
put up on a pedestal, has the lowest percentage  of workers to GDP of  any sector in the
economy. So if jobs are your problem, whic h they are in New Zealand, with the
unemployment rate being the hi ghest it has been since 1994 —at 6.8 percent—then this
is the last sector you would look at to be pr oviding jobs. It has the lowest percentage of
workers to GDP, and we know it is going to be  foreign workers. What we also know is
that the companies involved are predominantly offshore, so the profits are going to flow
offshore.
What we know is that for 100 percent of th e environmental risk we are going to see
the fourth-lowest Government  take in the world, we ar e going to see numerous tax
exemptions, we are going to see the profits fl ow offshore, and hardly any jobs for New
Zealanders. It does not stack  up. If you are going to pick winners, pick the smart
winners, look to the future, look to the smart economy. This is where the Government
could be going with its energy plan. We did not have to scrap the biofuel subsidy. The
Government did not have to scrap the solar hot-water grant scheme. In fact, what we
could be doing is providing a level playing field so re newables—clean energy—could
actually compete. The Government is quite happy to throw tens of millions of dollars in
subsidies through seismic surveys and free em issions trading scheme credits so the
taxpayer picks up the bill to subsidise this sector. But if you are going to pick winners,
why would you pick this sector when all the economics do not stack up? The smart
money internationally—in fact, the vast bulk of international investment according to
Bloomberg—is going into clean energy, not fossil fuels. This is the 21 st century
economy, not the 19 th century economy. What we can do is  invest in our assets and we
can use them to export. What we know is that  this Government is quite happy to pay for
solar plants in Tokelau and wind turbines in  Antarctica. We have all sorts of deals
around the world—we have Meridian exporting—but none for New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I would like to take
the time tonight to talk about  the renewables track  record for electricity generation in
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4367
New Zealand, because I think it is something that all New Zealanders can be
particularly proud of. But I would like to co rrect the last speaker, Gareth Hughes, who
was complaining about Taranaki. He was layi ng out that the oil and gas industry in
Taranaki is problematic because Taranaki ha s the lowest percentage of employment for
any region producing X amount of GDP. In ot her words, Taranaki produces a whole lot
of GDP—gross domestic product measured in ca sh—for the lowest number of jobs. He
was saying that what that means is that not many jobs are produced. What it actually
means is that the people are paid really we ll. The reason why the GDP per capita is so
high in Taranaki is that the average salary in Taranaki is upward of $75,000 a year.
In other words, what you have here is the Green Party advocating that it would rather
have more much-lower-paid jobs than ha ve higher-paid jobs. In Taranaki, where
unemployment is at the same level as acro ss the country, where the average wage and
salary is $75,000-plus, it can all be put down to the successful oil and gas industry in
that region, which has gone along happily for 50 years alongside dairy farming and
tourism. Have we ever heard a peep of a pr oblem out of Taranaki? No. But, apparently,
according to the Greens, now that National is  supporting its strategy of dairy farming,
tourism, and oil and gas exploration in Taranaki—something that has never been a
problem for five or six decades, but now Na tional is promoting that as, perhaps, a
strategy other regions could look at—the sky is  going to fall on our heads. That is what
is so ridiculous about that debate. Rather than talk about offshore, let us look at our
onshore experience. Taranaki has clearly done it successfully for many decades, and
there is no reason why it cannot be repeated sensibly elsewhere.
Seventy-seven percent of our electricity generation in New Zealand is done through
renewables. That is something I do not thi nk most New Zealanders know. Fifty-eight
percent of it is hydro, about  13 percent is geothermal , and 4.5 percent is wind
generation. That is a stunning record. I think it is in the top two or three in the world,
although I stand to be corrected. Norway is way up there with something like 99 percent
of electricity generation being renewable. Interestingly, the economy of Norway, which
has renewable electricity generation—good fo r them, very clean and green—is built off
the back of a very successf ul oil and gas industry in a place called the North Sea.
Norway—can you think of a cleaner, gr eener country—actually has oil and gas
exploration. Its economy is built off the back of it, and it is a very successful society,
indeed. So, yes, you can have renewable electricity generation and all those good things,
and a successful oil and gas industry, which, by the way, means you can drive along in a
car, catch an aeroplane, jump on a number of trains that are powered in that way, and do
a whole bunch of other things like make plastics, make fridges, make sofas, and
everything else you do with oil or using the energy of oil and gas.
We have a proud record in New Zealand. We want to reach 90 percent renewable
electricity generation by 2025. At 77 percent in  the last year, I believe, we are heading
that way. It could dip a bit this year because the hydro levels have been low, so we have
had to burn a bit more gas, but on the whole we are tracking in the right direction.
Conservation, of course, is also part of that story. I will not spend the time talking too
much about the extension of our insulation scheme. Over 4 years 188,000 houses across
New Zealand were to be insulated—that is, 188,000 private house owners able to access
subsidies from this Government to insula te their houses. We have extended that to
240,000 houses across New Zealand. This means it will run out a bit over 4 years, and
next year, of course, we are going to have to make a Budget decision about whether we
extend that or not. But it is a successful st ory—the renewable electricity generation, the
conservation measures around the insulation of housing and, of course, insulating every
State house in the country that can be insu lated across New Zealand next year, and our
promotion of our oil and gas industry.
4368 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
Vote agreed to.
Vote Housing
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : New Zealand First want s a robust Government
housing effort, for three primary reasons. Fi rstly, to meet the housing shortage. The
Government is not doing nearly enough to  see that housing needs throughout the
country are met. Auckland and Christchurch  are the problem areas, as most people
know. In Auckland, of course, there are the usual growth problems. Not enough is being
done to ensure an adequate supply of land, and not enough is being done to ensure
adequate housing stock, either . In Christchurch, of course , the Government really has
underestimated the immediate housing need. Land is becoming available for the future,
but there is especially a short-term deficit in housing stock. That is a real shortage that is
driving up rents and that is undeniable, although Ministers in  this House have tried to
deny that during question time in recent weeks. The second purpose is to make rental
housing affordable and accessible to people on the lowest incomes. The third, we
believe, is that we must make sure in th is country that we put  a regime of legal
minimum housing standards in place. That is also an urgent priority.
But turning to the Government’s social housing programmes, the Productivity

items.speaker: Commission stated recently
items.text: “Although the fo rmal objectives of the SHU”—the social
housing unit—“are clear, its structure as a semi-autonomous body leaves room for
unclear priorities, mixed purposes and misa ligned accountabilities.”  The Minister of
Finance failed to answer why that is in a recent question I put to him in this House.
Those questions—those issues—need an answ er, because there is a large amount of
money to be spent by way of grants in this area. The Minister must explain what the
priorities are, what the purpose of the fundi ng is, how those purposes will be achieved,
and what the outcomes sought are to be. Most of all, the Minister must show that the
need for a robust regime of accountability is met, and how that will be met. Instead, we
have had a deafening silence about all of those things, and the Productivity Commission
was correct to raise the matter.
I have other further specific questions. What  about the application processes, when
the Salvation Army is turned down for not m eeting financial criteri a but part of the $3
million M āori fund was allocated to the Whangare i Accessible Housing Trust, which
was running at a loss? That does not make se nse. Another question is this: what about
the competency of third sector housing provi ders applying to the Social Housing Unit
for the $104 million allocated in the 2012 B udget? These grants are given, for large
amounts of money, to organisations that wi ll own the housing that is funded. How do
we know that that is going to be well spent?  There are no State assets in return. What
happens if a recipient organisation fails ? Where do the assets go? There are many
unanswered questions like that.

items.speaker: Another question is this
items.text: how transparen t and accountable are the Social Housing
Unit processes for allocating funding to comm unity providers? The answer, I think, is
that they are as clea r as a mud house. That  is not good enough for a programme of this
size. Another question is what safeguards or risk management have been put in place for
the $104 million allo cated to non-profit NGOs a nd community social housing
providers? We need to be sure that they are risk-averse in their programmes and that
they are financially sound. We have been given no such information or assurances.

items.speaker: Another question is this
items.text: will well-mean ing community providers have enough
experience in the housing market, when private investors have lost millions of dollars in
the building and property market?

items.speaker: My conclusion from the current situation is this
items.text: the State would be better to provide
State housing directly and not rely so much on the NGO sector. The Government is too
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4369
focused on party political agendas, and not enough on real social housing outcomes, not
enough on value for money, and not enough on the interests of the taxpayer. Its
processes, priorities, accountabilities , and allocation processes are sloppy and
inadequate. Housing will suffer, and the taxpayer will be poorly served.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am very pleased to rise to take a call in this
estimates debate on Vote Housing. I think it would be fair to say that it has not been a
banner year for housing. The appropriati ons outlined in Budget 2012 certainly do not
engender much confidence that the next financial year will be any better.
There can be little doubt that we are f acing a multifaceted housing crisis in New
Zealand. This is a crisis of affordability, with rents rapidly increasing in most major
centres. In fact, in our largest city Auckland an estimation earlier this year that Statistics
New Zealand prepared for the Auckland Council suggested that there were 85,000
homes in which the tenants were payi ng unaffordable rents. The dream of
homeownership is out of reach for many thousands of New Zealanders of my
generation, who find that the dr eam of owning their own home is something they can
only aspire to. It is also a crisis of availability, with thousands on Housing New Zealand
Corporation waiting lists. Those waiting lists have themselves been magically reduced
by simply removing two categories from the lis ts, which makes it very easy to chop off
large numbers at once. But those who are st ill on the lists are wa iting, and there are
many of them.
Those who have been chopped off the lists are now battling it out in the private rental
market, which is becoming increasingly diffi cult. Private rentals are oversubscribed,
with hundreds of people showing up for every open home or responding to listings, and
finding that landlords really are able to take their pick of their tenants. If you have pets
or children, or other challenging circumstances, you can pretty much guarantee that you
are going to go straight to th e bottom of the list when it comes to looking for a private
rental property. There are not enough homes to meet the needs of New Zealanders.
Recently, another estimate in Auckland sugg ested that there is a shortage of 70,000
homes in Auckland alone.
It is also a crisis of quali ty, with hundreds of thousands  of children living in cold,
damp homes that are making them sick, a nd that is both in Housing New Zealand
Corporation properties and in private rentals. The full eff ect, I believe, of the leaky
homes crisis is also yet to be felt in terms of the qual ity of housing in New Zealand.
Nowhere are these crises of affordability, availability, and quality more apparent than in
our largest city Auckland and in our second-largest city Ch ristchurch, where they have
been compounded by the devastating impact and aftermath of the earthquakes.
So within that context of a housing crisis I want to address a specific issue, which is
how Housing New Zealand Corporation is co ping with its “Smarter. Faster. Fairer.”
reform programme, particularly from the pers pective of how it is delivering for tenants.
I want to focus on quality and maintena nce, and question whether Housing New
Zealand Corporation tenants,  who are, by the Minister’s  and the Government’s own
reckoning, only the most vulnerable families, are being provided for, and whether they
are living in adequate, warm, safe conditions.
We heard some time frames from the Mini ster in question time today in response to
questions that I asked. He said that when Housing New Zealand Corporation receives an
urgent request for health and safety maintenance, that should be dealt with within 4
hours. When it receives a request for urgent maintenance, that should be dealt with
within 2 days. And when it receives a genera l maintenance request that has credibility,
as the Minister would say, that should be dealt with within 10 days.
Despite the fact that 2 weeks ago in a written question to the Minister he told me that
he cannot “give an accurate indication of how mu ch work is still to be completed at any
4370 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
one time.”—and if anyone would like to look up that an swer, they can look up question
for written answer No. 4914—today he told  the House that Housing New Zealand
Corporation in fact meets these time frames 93 percent of the time. I wonder what has
changed in the last 2 weeks between when the Minister was unable to provide us an
estimate of how many maintenance reque sts were outstanding, and today, when
apparently 93 percent of the time they are magically being met.
But if we put that to one side and look at  the experiences of th e tenants, you really
would have to question whether this 93 perc ent is an accurate figure. I believe the
Minister may be confusing two things. I th ink he is confusing the difference between
response times, in terms of lodging a reque st and actually having that lodged in the
Housing New Zealand Corporation system, and perhaps somebody making a phone call
about it, and job completion—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The Green Party has used its allocation of
speeches now. This is just a point, because it is not only the Gree n Party, but also New
Zealand First. I note further down on the list that you are actually going to seek some
calls, but you have now used a ll your allocation, just as New Zealand First has. That is
the reason I pulled you up here. So if you want to take other calls, then you will need to
negotiate with the other parties. Unfortunately, I cannot give you a call, yet I note on the
schedule here that you are wanting to take calls in other votes.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I understand
that we have still got two cal ls. I understand that we have got one of Mana ’s calls. It
might be best to approach the Table to discuss it.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Yes, certainly Mana’s call has been
allocated to the Greens, but according to my schedule you are actually wanting more
than that. If that is not the case, you might like to come up here so we can discuss that
further.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I appreciate the comments made by
the member Holly Walker, and her questi ons today, of course . The invitation from
question time still stands: if she would like me to  look into those th ings, she should get
in contact with me directly and I can put  those through to the Housing New Zealand
Corporation and we might be able to get so me answers for her. I am very happy to do
that.
Generally, across the housing portfolio, we ha ve got social housing, then the private
rental markets, first-home buyers in thei r first homes, and then other housing, where
people have bought their second or third home, their home for life or whatever it is. So
there is sort of a housing c ontinuum there. We are part icularly interested as a
Government, as I know other parties are, in the bottom end, where people are struggling
the most—they might need State housing, or they might need housing by another
community housing provider that  provides other services su ch as mental health or
district nursing services, or parole help b ecause they might be recently released from
prison, or whatever it is—right through to the first-home buyer market.
But in that section of Stat e housing we have got a real challenge in the Government.
The previous Government had it as well, and any future Government of any hue will.
That is the fact that many of the Stat e houses were built in the 1940s and 1950s, and
many are in the wrong towns in this country —at least, there are too many in some
towns and not enough in others, such as Auck land. We can name some other places as
well, and it will be no surprise to anyone. Also, because the houses are so old, they are
in need of significant repair, and also ma ny are the wrong size. They are three-bedroom
houses, and, actually, these days  people often live alone or they have very, very large
families, so we need one or two-bedroom houses, and four, five, or six-bedroom houses
for large families.
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4371
I have talked about this for some time and laid out to this Parliament that that is a big
issue. Yes, people might like it to be res ponded to overnight, but we are talking about
70,000 State houses here, many of which are hou sing the most vulnerable. I would have
to say that every time we go to shift someone out of a State h ouse to repair it or to bowl
it and rebuild a nicer one, th e Green Party or the Labour Party oppose that. On the one
hand, in Tāmaki, for example, we have got almost 3,000 State houses up there, many on
quarter-acre and half-acre s ections, many very, very old and in a serious state of
disrepair, and many in places where families who are on the waiting list would love to
live. But when we go in there to do a massive development like T āmaki and start
removing the old houses to rebuild new State houses—houses for the community
housing sector, houses for first-home buyers, and so forth—the Labour Party is upset
about it. Well, you cannot bowl and rebuild a house without moving a family out to an
alternative State house. I must say that in most cases tenants ar e offered, if at all
possible, an alternative State house where th ey would like it, whic h is often close to
where they are now, and sometimes in a completely different neighbourhood.
What I am laying out for the Committee is  that if you want these housing upgrades,
which we do, if you want to spend the money, which we do, and if you want to build
new as much as possible, which we do, then there needs to be a degree of change.
Change is difficult, and we need to understand the fact that that is difficult for families,
and you cannot just do it overnight. But we are doing that in Tāmaki, we will be doing it
in Christchurch, and we are doing it in ot her areas of the countr y, and we have just
simply got to move forward.
It is also important to understand that many of the State houses across the portfolio
are not insulated. In fact, through the previ ous Labour Government, it did not seem to
have a particular focus on insulating State houses. Those members are beating the drum
in the Labour Party that we should for ce landlords and homeowners right across New
Zealand now to insulate thei r houses, yet they sat there w ith thousands of State houses
uninsulated during their three 3-year terms—their 9 years. We are saying no: we will
insulate every State house in New Zeal and that can be insulated. Many you cannot
insulate, but all the ones that can be insulated we want to insulate. We believe that it is
best to put the Government’s housing stock in order before we stand on some sort of
moral platform and say that everyone else has to do it. So the Labour Party and the
Green Party need to check themselves, and ask themselves the question why they never
insulated every State house in the country, yet under a Na tional Government we are
doing it. And we should be finished by the end of next year. We will be insulating State
houses, we are proud of the fact that we ar e insulating them, and we will be upgrading
State houses.
We support the community housing sector. In fact, one of the things we do with the
community housing sector is make sure that  when it builds a house it is well insulated,
of course—because the laws say so—but also it is including other things like wide
doorways and wide passageways, wherever possible, so that they are easily adjusted. So
we are doing a lot of work in housing. It is taking a lot of work, and we would
appreciate everyone’s support.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Conservation

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chairperson. The summary of new policy
initiatives in the performance information fo r Vote Conservation is the story of funding
cuts, and it is yet another example of the anti-environment stance and policies of this
Government. In Vote Conservation we see $8.7 million axed from the purchase and
development of new reserves to meet the G overnment’s cost-saving target. We see $1.5
4372 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
million cut from natural heritage management. Those are the programmes to care for
our public conservation lands, for threatened species, and for pest and weed control.
That means there will be six fewer possum c ontrol operations done than in the previous
financial year. We see a $1 million cut in th e management of recreational opportunities,
so that means fewer kilometres of walk ing and tramping tracks are maintained, and
fewer pamphlets promoting the opportunities to go walking and mountain biking on
conservation land.
If the $1.67 million that the Ministry of  Economic Development wasted surveying
the unlikely mineral potential of Te W āhipounamu - South West New Zealand World
Heritage Area had gone to the Department of Conservation, it could have paid for more
than 100,000 hectares of aerial pest control to protect mistletoe, r ātā, and fuchsia from
possum browse and to improve the prospects fo r threatened species such as the rowi or
the Haast brown kiwi. The funding cuts that we see in this vote combined with the
policy direction that we see in the Department  of Conservation’s statement of intent are
worrying. The department is signalling that  conservation lands are open for business,
and that includes some quite destructive extractive businesses.
The department’s statement of intent has a major section on business opportunities.
One of the initiatives in that section is to  “increase the number, value, and quality of
commercial ‘sponsorship’ partners providi ng net benefit to conservation.” The
Department of Conservation already has a business relationship with five major
corporates: Mitre 10, Rio Tinto, BNZ, Solid  Energy, and Genesis. Those companies
generated a mere $2.5 million in sponsorship  revenue in the 2010-11 financial year.
That is paltry, given their size and given the major public relations benefits that
companies such as BNZ have had from  the kiwi recovery programme, where
departmental employees have had to wear BNZ-branded clothing when they are filmed
or photographed working with kiwi. The G overnment’s cuts to  conservation funding
mean that the department is putting out its be gging bowl to the corporate sector to help
meet that funding shortfall.
The statement of intent does not include any specific targ ets, but this is a very
worrying initiative, particularly when we hear the reports that  the department is
considering accepting sponsorship from Fonterra . This is troubling, because Fonterra’s
shareholders are responsible for some of th e most extensive, seri ous, and severe water
pollution problems in New Zealand. That is from agricultura l intensification,
particularly dairying expansion in the lowla nd areas, and the impact that is having on
our lowland streams. So the department need s to be very careful when it enters into
sponsorship arrangements.
Fonterra does not operate on conservation land, and any sponsorship arrangement is
potential “greenwash” for the company. If  Fonterra sponsors the Department of
Conservation, this raises que stions about what Fonterra would expect in return—what
compromises the department would have to  make to its stat utory advocacy—because
under this National Government the Depart ment of Conservation has cut back its
Resource Management Act advocacy for nature outside the conservation estate.
Despite the R ākaia water conservation order recognising that that river has
outstanding values as habitat for braided rive r birds such as the black-fronted tern and
the wrybill plover—both threatened species—t he department has not been involved in
TrustPower’s application to amend the wate r conservation order a nd change the river’s
flows. The department had a major role in th e first generation of di strict and regional
plans. Working with conservation groups, it go t rules controlling indigenous vegetation
clearance, wetland drainage, and stock access to waterw ays. In Canterbury, the
Environment Canterbury commissioners have just notified the combined land and water
regional plan for Canterbury.
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4373
If Fonterra becomes a commercial sponsor  of the Department of Conservation, will
this constrain the department’s already limited Resource Management Act advocacy?
Will the department seek stronger policies, in  that plan and other plans, to protect the
habitats of native fish, will it oppose irriga tion takes, or will it wind back its limited
advocacy?

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am pleased to take a call
on the estimates for Vote Conservation. Contrary  to what the previous speaker, Eugenie
Sage, has spoken about, the actual expenditure  for the Department of Conservation has
increased over the last 6 years. The appropriation is $444.9 million for 2012-13, and
that is slightly up on the actual expenditu re of $437.8 million in 2011-12. Actually, that
expenditure has been trending up for the last  6 years and is now almost double what it
Vote Conservation is appropriated to support the Department of Conservation, which
has a goal of encouraging all New Zealanders to enjoy the conserva tion estate, to gain
the benefits from a healthy, functioning ecosystem, to experience its recreational
opportunities, and to appreciate our historic  heritage. The biggest expenses are the
management of the natural environment, and the Department of Conservation spends
$156.3 million per year on that, and the manageme nt of recreational opportunities, with
an expenditure of $145.7 million and a capital expenditure of $59 million.
New Zealanders are totally committed to our country being clean and green, and they
really do enjoy getting into the great outdoors and being part of our conservation estate.
The conservation estate that this appropriati on covers is 8 million hectares of land. It
includes 34 marine reserves and six marine ma mmal sanctuaries. Of course, it is a huge
job to manage, to protect, and to conserve this environment. There will never be enough
money to do all the good work that we woul d like to do. So the department is really
working hard and thinking smart about how to  stretch its dollars. It is working at
developing partnerships to increase that conservation dollar.
Over $17 million of Crown revenue comes fr om a third-party income, and that is
generated from the permissions granted by the Department of Conservation for
commercial activity on conservation land. Th is commercial activity often has a win-
win. It is things like horse trekking, whale watching, glacie r climbing, cycle trails, bus
tours, camping grounds—hundreds of recr eational opportunities and tourism
experiences. These concessions get people out  on to the conservation estate. They get
them interested in the environment. They allow them to enjoy and appreciate our great
outdoors, and provide income so we can look after it.
I was very pleased to see that in the review the Minister of Conservation is looking at
the returns on concessions to ensure that we get the best possible return from the
commercial use of our conservation estate. It was interesting that Eugenie Sage talked
about conservation partnerships. Partnerships with corporates are becoming increasingly
popular. They seem to be particularly keen on supporting our iconic birds. The kiwi, the
kākāpō, the k ōkako, and even the p ūkeko have their own projects. And then dollars
invested by New Zealand businesses mean that  the taxpayer’s conservation dollars can
go even further.
I think we have all been captured by Sirocco the k ākāpō. He is the face—or, should I
say, the beak—of the K ākāpō Recovery Programme. He can  be seen advocating that
recovery programme on Facebook and Twitter.  He has a lot of public appearances
around the country. The Kākāpō Recovery Programme has been sponsored by Rio Tinto
Alcan since 1990. When it took that programme out, there were only 50 birds alive, and
there was a real feeling that they may face extinction. Rio Tinto Alcan has worked hard
with the Department of Conservation and th e Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society,
and there are now 129 adult birds. They ha ve a goal to establish 150 adult breeding
4374 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
females, and they are on their way towards th at. Rio Tinto Alcan’s su pport is financial,
of course, but it is also pr actical and strategic. The k ākāpō and all of us who value this
special bird are the beneficiaries of th at. Air New Zealand too has always been
particularly supportive of conservation projects.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I am delighted to join in this debate on
the Appropriation (2012/13 Estimates) Bill fo r Vote Conservation. My colleague from
the Green Party Eugenie Sage talked about the huge damage that is being done to our
conservation estate as a result of the signifi cant funding cuts. It is interesting now that
the National Government is talking about the funding over 6 year s—6 years. It has
suddenly extended its time. It will make it look better, unless people remember what
year National was elected and do the real maths, which I think most New Zealanders
will do.
Eugenie Sage was referring to the funding cu ts and to what a dr amatic decrease will
mean for areas like possum control, where we will no longer be able to have the possum
control that we need. Not long ago the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment talked about our forests becoming silent as a result of a lack of investment
in possum control. This is the very future th at we are facing as a result of the lack of
attention, lack of focus, and lack of inve stment shown by the National Government. We
know too in developing access to our recreatio nal facilities, our conservation estate, and
our public land that unless there is  that investment they will just fall into disrepair. We
have seen that with our huts, we have seen th at with tracks, and we have seen that with
information brochures. We know the impact th at it has, not just on our tourism industry
but also on New Zealanders, who still—and I support this—expect that access to our
public lands is a right that Ne w Zealanders can enjoy. It is good for us, we love it, and
we should be able to continue it.
The other part of this portfolio vote that I find very disappointing is the fact that
when you look at all the portfolio s, conservation is r eally one of the l eaders in terms of
the challenges and the opportunitie s, as well as the responsibility, that it presents to the
Minister, and on all three of those takes the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkinson,
has just really shrugged her shoulders and said  it is all too hard. She has walked away
from any responsibility she has as the leader  of the protection a nd management of our
conservation estate. The Nationa l Party has a constant mantra  that conservation and the
economy are a balance—that we have to ba lance our conservation values against our
economic outcomes. It does the same on the envi ronment. Well, my view of that is that
when it comes to conservation and the envi ronment, this Government—the National
Government—knows the price of everything and the value of nothing. It says that there
is this balance between the economy and c onservation. Well, it is a false dichotomy.
There is no economy in New Zealand without  our conservation estate. We know that
National’s approach is narrow-minded and it is  short term, and it will mean that more
New Zealanders will lose their jobs in the longer term.
National’s view that the environment and the economy are in this locked battle to the
death is a view from the last century. It is not a view for the current times or a vision for
the future. And that last century is the same  century that gave us the failed asset sales
programme—exactly the same programme th at this current Government is going
through. That is not the view that Labour holds. We view co nservation as a strength of
our economy, as a critical part of the overall  health and well-being of New Zealanders.
It is not an asset to be flogged off at the earliest convenience.
As a result of Kate Wilkinson, the Minister , walking away from her responsibility,
we have now seen subspecies like the M āui’s dolphin with only 55 of that species left.
That is not just in our waters, and not just  in Australasia, but on the planet. You cannot
get much closer to extincti on than having only 55 animals left, yet when the Minister,
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4375
along with her colleague the Minister for Pr imary Industries, had an opportunity to do
something positive about this critically endang ered species, they did as little as they
possibly could. Not only does that put M āui’s dolphins at an immediate and distinct risk
of extinction, but also what has happened is that, internationally, countries are looking
at us and saying: “How is Ne w Zealand so backward that it doesn’t have sustainable
fishing practices?”, and now our fishing industry is at risk, as well.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I just want to pick up where
my colleague the Hon Ruth Dyson, our exce llent conservation spoke sperson, left off.
The Minister of Conservation has also christened herself,  I think, the “Minister for
Looking”—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Just looking.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: —just looking—because that is what Kate Wilkinson told
a select committee when peopl e raised concerns about wh ether it was a good idea for
this Government to go on a search of World Heritage sites for mining opportunities.

items.speaker: Kate Wilkinson said
items.text: “Nothing to do with me. I’m just the ‘Minister for Looking’. I’m
not the Minister responsible for the drilling or the digging; I’m just the ‘Minister for
Looking’.”
What I would like the Minister of Conservati on to be is the “Minister for Doing”. I
would like the Minister of C onservation to actually get out there and do something to
protect the conservation estate. I would like the Minister of Conservation to actually get
out there and do something about threatened sp ecies, but instead all we have seen from
this Minister of Conservation and conservation under this Government is funding cuts—
no sense of the value of the conservation estate to New Zealand, no sense of its intrinsic
value to New Zealand and New Zealanders, and no sense of its real economic value.
The numbers tell a story. In the 2009 Budget $54 million was taken out of the
conservation budget, and that has its impact y ear on year on year. But then we come to
this year’s Budget, with a further $11 m illion taken out of the conservation budget—a
further $11 million that the Department of C onservation has to find, has to cut from the
services that are being provi ded to New Zealand and to our conservation estate. But
there is good news coming for the Department of Conservation. Next year it gets only
an $8.7 million cut. So there we go; the Gove rnment in its generosity says: “No, next
year it’ll just be $8.7 million more that the Department of Conservation has to cut.”
We have been told time and again by this Government that these cuts are back-office
cuts and nothing will be happening on the front line. Well, let us look at where staffing
cuts have come from in the Department of Conservation, as pa rt of the $54 million
reduction in that first 2009 Budget: 21 staff cu t in Nelson, 18 staff cut in the Waikato,
12 staff cut in Wanganui, and around 12 to 15 staff cut in Southland. These are the
people at the front line of conservation in New Zealand. These are the people losing
their jobs under National.
This is not some back-office cut. These are not some services that New Zealanders
will not see. These are the people in our regions who are doing the work that New
Zealanders know is important and that tour ists see every day and say: “Isn’t it
tremendous that you’ve got that Department of  Conservation that is looking after what
makes New Zealand beautiful.” They are the pe ople in our regions. It is those jobs that
are going. That is what this Budget has done. It  has continued Nationa l’s cuts to a vital
public service agency, the Depa rtment of Conservation, not in some back office in
Wellington but out there in the regions of New Zealand.
Part of those cuts were to scientists. There is not much more front line for the
Department of Conservation than the science that it does. Hundreds of scientists wrote
to this Government and said: “Recessions  come and go; extinction is forever.”—
extinction is forever. Only around 200 of the 2, 700 threatened specie s in this country
4376 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012
are actually currently being monitored by th e Department of Conservation, and that
goes down every year. Ruth Dyson has alre ady mentioned what is happening with
possum control. The Department of Conservation is now able to look at only 1.2 million
of the 8.5 million hectares it covers for possum control.
This Government is hamstringing the De partment of Conservation from doing its
core functions, and it is hidi ng that under the rhetoric of saying: “We’re going to cut
back on bureaucracy.” Nothing about that statem ent is true. All that we see in front of
us is cuts to the services that the De partment of Conservation provides, and New
Zealanders will be worse off as a result . We will be worse off in terms of the
environment that we live in, in terms of the biodiversity of this country, and we will
actually be worse off in terms of our tourism.
Then it goes to the most ludicrous extent, because now the so-called partnerships that
the Department of Conservation is undertak ing are being forced on it because it does
not have the money to do its co re business. It is privatising looking after the kiwi. What
is more New Zealand than looking after the kiwi? Yet that is now being privatised. This
Budget is letting down New Zealand when it comes to core conservation values and
looking after our environment.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Food Safety agreed to.
House resumed.
The Chairperson reported progress on the Appropriation (2012/13 Estimates) Bill
and no progress on the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental
Effects) Bill.
Report adopted.
