14 Aug 2012 Motions 4289 
TUESDAY, 14 AUGUST 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
New Zealand Defence Force—Deaths of Lance Corporals Pralli Durrer and Rory 
Malone in Afghanistan 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Acting Prime Minister) : I seek leave to move a motion 
without notice on the in cident on Saturday, 4 August 201 2 in the Bamian Province of 
Afghanistan that tragically claimed the lives  of two New Zealand soldiers and injured 
six more. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I move, That this House express  its deep sympathy and 
condolences to the family, friends, and milita ry colleagues of the New Zealand Army 
soldiers killed in Afghanistan on 4 August, and  also express its sy mpathy to their six 
injured colleagues and its best wishes for their recovery.  On Saturday, 4 August at 
around 8 a.m. local time memb ers of the New Zealand De fence Force’s provincial 
reconstruction team responded to a request for assistance from an Afghan quick reaction 
force platoon, which had come under insurg ent attack in north- east Bamian. A New 
Zealand Defence Force patrol was immediately mobilised and assisted in engaging the 
insurgents until a second New Zealand Defence Force patrol arrived. It too came under 
attack, during which some of our personne l were wounded. Two further New Zealand 
patrols arrived, and during the ensuing fi re fight the New Zealand Defence Force 
sustained more casualties, including Lance Corporal Rory Malone, who was killed at 
the scene. Seven wounded were evacuated, and the most seriously injured soldier, 
Lance Corporal Pralli Durrer, died en route to hospital. 
 This incident has served as a tragic reminder of the risks that our men and women in 
the services face every day in unstable conflict zones. Rory Malone and Pralli Durrer 
are the sixth and seventh Kiwis to die wh ile working selflessly on behalf of New 
Zealand and the international community in trying to stabilise Afghanistan. These Kiwis 
are willing to risk their lives defending not their homeland but strangers in another 
country. We could not ask more of them. We could not expect more of them.  
The Government has received messages from  many other Governments and leaders 
who understand the terrible sacrifices that  are being made in Afghanistan as we 
collectively do our best to cr eate a functioning, stable society there. We have always 
known that the task is both vital and dange rous. I know that for the Defence Force and 
their families, accepting that there are risks in  the job is part of daily life. However, I 
also know that that knowledge does not make it any easier when the knock at the door 
that they hope will never come does come . The weekend before last it came for the 
Durrers and the Malones, and also for their friends and colleagues inside and outside the 
Defence Force, and for the Government and the people of New Zealand. On Saturday I 
attended the memorial service for Pralli Du rrer and Rory Malone, and the more I learn 
about them, the more heavily their loss weighs.  
We are mindful today also of the injured. I am advised that three of the six returned 
to their families in New Zealand late yesterday. Three more remain in hospital in 
Germany, all in a stable condition. One of them is Major Craig Wilson, who was the 
commanding officer of the team involved in the attack. He has strongly praised the 
courage and the performance of Lance Cor porals Durrer and Malone in the combat 
4290 Motions 14 Aug 2012 
engagement that claimed their lives. It is hard to find any redeeming feature in this 
tragedy, but at least in  today’s conflicts we ar e usually able to repa triate our fallen, and 
the Government thanks the United States G overnment for its assistance in evacuating 
the wounded and returning Rory Malone and Pralli Durrer to their families. 
Bamian is a better place because of the de dication, effort, and commitment of these 
men and their colleagues. Their sacrifice has been a dreadful price to pay, but a 
reminder too of why we are there. Violence,  lawlessness, and a brutal and wilful 
disregard of the rights of others should neve r be allowed to become a way of life. These 
two young, brave men were fighting for a more secure Afghanistan and a more secure 
world. We are proud of them and their colleag ues, who right now as I speak are facing 
the same risks to uphold the same noble objectives. The Malone and Durrer families’ 
loss is New Zealand’s loss. We grieve for them and with them. 
DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) : On Saturday I attended the 
memorial service for the two brave, young Ne w Zealand soldiers who tragically lost 
their lives on 4 August while serving in Afghanistan. It was a moving experience to 
hear the families of Lance Co rporal Pralli Durrer and Lance Corporal Rory Malone talk 
about the contribution these men made to th eir communities, to the Defence Force, and 
to our country. Both of their commanders s poke also of their enthusiasm in the army 
and the respect they earned from their mates who served alongside them. Their families 
are proud of them and so are we as a nation.  
Rory Malone is remembered as a quiet st udent with a wicked sense of humour who 
just got on with things. His steady determination continued when he entered the army in 
2002. His great-great-grandfather Lieutenant Colonel William Malone was the 
commanding officer of the Wellington Infantry  Battalion at Gallipoli who died at 
Chunuk Bair. He led his troops with much bravery. Rory showed the same family 
courage under fire. He repor tedly dragged his company co mmander to safety before, 
sadly, losing his life helping another fallen comrade caught up in the battle.  
Pralli Durrer was a Southern Man, born in Invercargill, growing up in Christchurch. 
He is still remembered at his primary school  as being a shining star. He survived the 
initial attacks, supporting his comrades under fire. Sadly, he was wounded, and passed 
away en route to the base at Bagram.  
These soldiers made the ultimate sacrifice. They lost their lives doing what they 
believed in, and we will  always remember them for that . They are our heroes. Six other 
New Zealand soldiers were also injured in the attack. We wish them a speedy recovery. 
We also thank the Dutch, German, and American  air forces, which came to their aid in 
the aftermath of the attack.  
The deaths of these two young men come al most exactly 2 years to the day since 
New Zealand’s first fatality in Afghanistan, when Lieutenant Tim O’Donnell was killed 
in the same area during an attack on his patrol . It is fitting that we remember him today, 
along with all those New Zealanders who have died in Afghanistan and in other conflict 
zones around the world, serving our country. Th ey gave their lives trying to make the 
world a better place.  
Often these soldiers make an impact that  is largely unseen. We look at the Bamian 
Province. How many kids are alive today simply because their work allowed 
vaccinations to happen? How many women surv ived childbirth because stability in the 
province brought about by their efforts ensure d those women could get to hospital? Or 
the numbers of children—especially girls—who have attended school and now have 
possibilities for a much better life, more than they had before.  
We thank our soldiers for doing us pr oud, for contributing to peace, and for

JONATHAN YOUNG (National—New Plymouth): I am very pleased to stand and 
speak in this estimates debate regarding energy and resources. The Government has set 
ambitious economic goals for New Zealand, and that requires a significant improvement 
in our economic performance. Productivity improvements are incremental as we gain

Regarding the economic development of th is country, we have put together a 
business growth plan that will grow more and bigger businesses in New Zealand and 
provide the standard of living New Zealande rs aspire to. This business growth plan 
touches on six key areas: capital markets; innovation a nd ideas; skilled and safe 
workplaces; infrastructure, which includes elec tricity, broadband, and transport; export

heavily upon all six of these. Oil is our fourth-largest expo rt earner, with a value of

there is sort of a housing c ontinuum there. We are part icularly interested as a 
Government, as I know other parties are, in the bottom end, where people are struggling 
the most—they might need State housing, or they might need housing by another 
community housing provider that  provides other services su ch as mental health or 
district nursing services, or parole help b ecause they might be recently released from 
prison, or whatever it is—right through to the first-home buyer market.  
 But in that section of Stat e housing we have got a real challenge in the Government. 
The previous Government had it as well, and any future Government of any hue will. 
That is the fact that many of the Stat e houses were built in the 1940s and 1950s, and 
many are in the wrong towns in this country —at least, there are too many in some 
towns and not enough in others, such as Auck land. We can name some other places as 
well, and it will be no surprise to anyone. Also, because the houses are so old, they are 
in need of significant repair, and also ma ny are the wrong size. They are three-bedroom 
houses, and, actually, these days  people often live alone or they have very, very large 
families, so we need one or two-bedroom houses, and four, five, or six-bedroom houses 
for large families.  
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4371 
I have talked about this for some time and laid out to this Parliament that that is a big 
issue. Yes, people might like it to be res ponded to overnight, but we are talking about 
70,000 State houses here, many of which are hou sing the most vulnerable. I would have 
to say that every time we go to shift someone out of a State h ouse to repair it or to bowl 
it and rebuild a nicer one, th e Green Party or the Labour Party oppose that. On the one 
hand, in Tāmaki, for example, we have got almost 3,000 State houses up there, many on 
quarter-acre and half-acre s ections, many very, very old and in a serious state of 
disrepair, and many in places where families who are on the waiting list would love to 
live. But when we go in there to do a massive development like T āmaki and start 
removing the old houses to rebuild new State houses—houses for the community 
housing sector, houses for first-home buyers, and so forth—the Labour Party is upset 
about it. Well, you cannot bowl and rebuild a house without moving a family out to an 
alternative State house. I must say that in most cases tenants ar e offered, if at all 
possible, an alternative State house where th ey would like it, whic h is often close to 
where they are now, and sometimes in a completely different neighbourhood.  
What I am laying out for the Committee is  that if you want these housing upgrades, 
which we do, if you want to spend the money, which we do, and if you want to build 
new as much as possible, which we do, then there needs to be a degree of change. 
Change is difficult, and we need to understand the fact that that is difficult for families, 
and you cannot just do it overnight. But we are doing that in Tāmaki, we will be doing it 
in Christchurch, and we are doing it in ot her areas of the countr y, and we have just 
simply got to move forward.  
It is also important to understand that many of the State houses across the portfolio 
are not insulated. In fact, through the previ ous Labour Government, it did not seem to 
have a particular focus on insulating State houses. Those members are beating the drum 
in the Labour Party that we should for ce landlords and homeowners right across New 
Zealand now to insulate thei r houses, yet they sat there w ith thousands of State houses 
uninsulated during their three 3-year terms—their 9 years. We are saying no: we will 
insulate every State house in New Zeal and that can be insulated. Many you cannot 
insulate, but all the ones that can be insulated we want to insulate. We believe that it is 
best to put the Government’s housing stock in order before we stand on some sort of 
moral platform and say that everyone else has to do it. So the Labour Party and the 
Green Party need to check themselves, and ask themselves the question why they never 
insulated every State house in the country, yet under a Na tional Government we are 
doing it. And we should be finished by the end of next year. We will be insulating State 
houses, we are proud of the fact that we ar e insulating them, and we will be upgrading 
State houses.  
We support the community housing sector. In fact, one of the things we do with the 
community housing sector is make sure that  when it builds a house it is well insulated, 
of course—because the laws say so—but also it is including other things like wide 
doorways and wide passageways, wherever possible, so that they are easily adjusted. So 
we are doing a lot of work in housing. It is taking a lot of work, and we would 
appreciate everyone’s support.  
Vote agreed to. 
Vote Conservation 
EUGENIE SAGE (Green): Tēnā koe, Mr Chairperson. The summary of new policy 
initiatives in the performance information fo r Vote Conservation is the story of funding 
cuts, and it is yet another example of the anti-environment stance and policies of this 
Government. In Vote Conservation we see $8.7 million axed from the purchase and 
development of new reserves to meet the G overnment’s cost-saving target. We see $1.5 
4372 Estimates Debate 14 Aug 2012 
million cut from natural heritage management. Those are the programmes to care for 
our public conservation lands, for threatened species, and for pest and weed control. 
That means there will be six fewer possum c ontrol operations done than in the previous 
financial year. We see a $1 million cut in th e management of recreational opportunities, 
so that means fewer kilometres of walk ing and tramping tracks are maintained, and 
fewer pamphlets promoting the opportunities to go walking and mountain biking on 
conservation land.  
If the $1.67 million that the Ministry of  Economic Development wasted surveying 
the unlikely mineral potential of Te W āhipounamu - South West New Zealand World 
Heritage Area had gone to the Department of Conservation, it could have paid for more 
than 100,000 hectares of aerial pest control to protect mistletoe, r ātā, and fuchsia from 
possum browse and to improve the prospects fo r threatened species such as the rowi or 
the Haast brown kiwi. The funding cuts that we see in this vote combined with the 
policy direction that we see in the Department  of Conservation’s statement of intent are 
worrying. The department is signalling that  conservation lands are open for business, 
and that includes some quite destructive extractive businesses.  
The department’s statement of intent has a major section on business opportunities. 
One of the initiatives in that section is to  “increase the number, value, and quality of 
commercial ‘sponsorship’ partners providi ng net benefit to conservation.” The 
Department of Conservation already has a business relationship with five major 
corporates: Mitre 10, Rio Tinto, BNZ, Solid  Energy, and Genesis. Those companies 
generated a mere $2.5 million in sponsorship  revenue in the 2010-11 financial year. 
That is paltry, given their size and given the major public relations benefits that 
companies such as BNZ have had from  the kiwi recovery programme, where 
departmental employees have had to wear BNZ-branded clothing when they are filmed 
or photographed working with kiwi. The G overnment’s cuts to  conservation funding 
mean that the department is putting out its be gging bowl to the corporate sector to help 
meet that funding shortfall.  
The statement of intent does not include any specific targ ets, but this is a very 
worrying initiative, particularly when we hear the reports that  the department is 
considering accepting sponsorship from Fonterra . This is troubling, because Fonterra’s 
shareholders are responsible for some of th e most extensive, seri ous, and severe water 
pollution problems in New Zealand. That is from agricultura l intensification, 
particularly dairying expansion in the lowla nd areas, and the impact that is having on 
our lowland streams. So the department need s to be very careful when it enters into 
sponsorship arrangements.  
Fonterra does not operate on conservation land, and any sponsorship arrangement is 
potential “greenwash” for the company. If  Fonterra sponsors the Department of 
Conservation, this raises que stions about what Fonterra would expect in return—what 
compromises the department would have to  make to its stat utory advocacy—because 
under this National Government the Depart ment of Conservation has cut back its 
Resource Management Act advocacy for nature outside the conservation estate.  
Despite the R ākaia water conservation order recognising that that river has 
outstanding values as habitat for braided rive r birds such as the black-fronted tern and 
the wrybill plover—both threatened species—t he department has not been involved in 
TrustPower’s application to amend the wate r conservation order a nd change the river’s 
flows. The department had a major role in th e first generation of di strict and regional 
plans. Working with conservation groups, it go t rules controlling indigenous vegetation 
clearance, wetland drainage, and stock access to waterw ays. In Canterbury, the 
Environment Canterbury commissioners have just notified the combined land and water 
regional plan for Canterbury.  
14 Aug 2012 Estimates Debate 4373 
If Fonterra becomes a commercial sponsor  of the Department of Conservation, will 
this constrain the department’s already limited Resource Management Act advocacy? 
Will the department seek stronger policies, in  that plan and other plans, to protect the 
habitats of native fish, will it oppose irriga tion takes, or will it wind back its limited 
advocacy? 
NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central): I am pleased to take a call 
on the estimates for Vote Conservation. Contrary  to what the previous speaker, Eugenie 
Sage, has spoken about, the actual expenditure  for the Department of Conservation has 
increased over the last 6 years. The appropriation is $444.9 million for 2012-13, and 
that is slightly up on the actual expenditu re of $437.8 million in 2011-12. Actually, that 
expenditure has been trending up for the last  6 years and is now almost double what it 
was in 2001-02.  
Vote Conservation is appropriated to support the Department of Conservation, which 
has a goal of encouraging all New Zealanders to enjoy the conserva tion estate, to gain 
the benefits from a healthy, functioning ecosystem, to experience its recreational 
opportunities, and to appreciate our historic  heritage. The biggest expenses are the 
management of the natural environment, and the Department of Conservation spends 
$156.3 million per year on that, and the manageme nt of recreational opportunities, with 
an expenditure of $145.7 million and a capital expenditure of $59 million.  
New Zealanders are totally committed to our country being clean and green, and they 
really do enjoy getting into the great outdoors and being part of our conservation estate. 
The conservation estate that this appropriati on covers is 8 million hectares of land. It 
includes 34 marine reserves and six marine ma mmal sanctuaries. Of course, it is a huge 
job to manage, to protect, and to conserve this environment. There will never be enough 
money to do all the good work that we woul d like to do. So the department is really 
working hard and thinking smart about how to  stretch its dollars. It is working at 
developing partnerships to increase that conservation dollar.  
Over $17 million of Crown revenue comes fr om a third-party income, and that is 
generated from the permissions granted by the Department of Conservation for 
commercial activity on conservation land. Th is commercial activity often has a win-
win. It is things like horse trekking, whale watching, glacie r climbing, cycle trails, bus 
tours, camping grounds—hundreds of recr eational opportunities and tourism 
experiences. These concessions get people out  on to the conservation estate. They get 
them interested in the environment. They allow them to enjoy and appreciate our great 
outdoors, and provide income so we can look after it.  
I was very pleased to see that in the review the Minister of Conservation is looking at 
the returns on concessions to ensure that we get the best possible return from the 
commercial use of our conservation estate. It was interesting that Eugenie Sage talked 
about conservation partnerships. Partnerships with corporates are becoming increasingly 
popular. They seem to be particularly keen on supporting our iconic birds. The kiwi, the 
kākāpō, the k ōkako, and even the p ūkeko have their own projects. And then dollars 
invested by New Zealand businesses mean that  the taxpayer’s conservation dollars can 
go even further.  
I think we have all been captured by Sirocco the k ākāpō. He is the face—or, should I 
say, the beak—of the K ākāpō Recovery Programme. He can  be seen advocating that

around the country. The Kākāpō Recovery Programme has been sponsored by Rio Tinto

females, and they are on their way towards th at. Rio Tinto Alcan’s su pport is financial,

Hon RUTH DYSON (Labour—Port Hills): I am delighted to join in this debate on 
the Appropriation (2012/13 Estimates) Bill fo r Vote Conservation. My colleague from

 Eugenie Sage was referring to the funding cu ts and to what a dr amatic decrease will

Environment talked about our forests becoming silent as a result of a lack of investment

our public land that unless there is  that investment they will just fall into disrepair. We

public lands is a right that Ne w Zealanders can enjoy. It is good for us, we love it, and 
we should be able to continue it.  
The other part of this portfolio vote that I find very disappointing is the fact that 
when you look at all the portfolio s, conservation is r eally one of the l eaders in terms of 
the challenges and the opportunitie s, as well as the responsibility, that it presents to the 
Minister, and on all three of those takes the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkinson, 
has just really shrugged her shoulders and said  it is all too hard. She has walked away 
from any responsibility she has as the leader  of the protection a nd management of our 
conservation estate. The Nationa l Party has a constant mantra  that conservation and the 
economy are a balance—that we have to ba lance our conservation values against our

when it comes to conservation and the envi ronment, this Government—the National 
Government—knows the price of everything and the value of nothing. It says that there 
is this balance between the economy and c onservation. Well, it is a false dichotomy.

National’s view that the environment and the economy are in this locked battle to the

the future. And that last century is the same  century that gave us the failed asset sales 
programme—exactly the same programme th at this current Government is going 
through. That is not the view that Labour holds. We view co nservation as a strength of 
our economy, as a critical part of the overall  health and well-being of New Zealanders. 
It is not an asset to be flogged off at the earliest convenience.  
As a result of Kate Wilkinson, the Minister , walking away from her responsibility, 
we have now seen subspecies like the M āui’s dolphin with only 55 of that species left. 
That is not just in our waters, and not just  in Australasia, but on the planet. You cannot 
get much closer to extincti on than having only 55 animals left, yet when the Minister,

GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour) : I just want to pick up where

GRANT ROBERTSON: —just looking—because that is what Kate Wilkinson told

Kate Wilkinson said: “Nothing to do with me. I’m just the ‘Minister for Looking’. I’m

What I would like the Minister of Conservati on to be is the “Minister for Doing”. I

are going. That is what this Budget has done. It  has continued Nationa l’s cuts to a vital 
public service agency, the Depa rtment of Conservation, not in some back office in 
Wellington but out there in the regions of New Zealand.  
Part of those cuts were to scientists. There is not much more front line for the 
Department of Conservation than the science that it does. Hundreds of scientists wrote 
to this Government and said: “Recessions  come and go; extinction is forever.”—
extinction is forever. Only around 200 of the 2, 700 threatened specie s in this country

This Government is hamstringing the De partment of Conservation from doing its
